March 2 – March 5, 2027: Winners are announced, and award notifications are sent. Why Join the PCBWay × Tindie AI Hardware Design Contest? This contest is more than just a competition. It's an opportunity to experiment with AI, develop practical hardware skills, and share your creativity with a global community. Registration and project submissions open on November 1, 2026 (PT). Get your ideas ready and join the challenge! About the PCBWay × Tindie AI Hardware Design Contest Artificial intelligence is creating new possibilities for hardware development. From intelligent sensors and smart home devices to robotics and edge AI applications, AI is changing how electronic devices interact with people and the world around them. The PCBWay × Tindie AI Hardware Design Contest aims to encourage makers and developers to explore these possibilities through practical hardware projects. By combining PCBWay's PCB manufacturing and engineering capabilities with Tindie's hardware maker community, we hope to support innovative ideas and help more creators turn their concepts into real-world products. Whether you're an experienced hardware engineer or an independent maker exploring AI for the first time, you're welcome to participate. Project Ideas and Inspiration What can you build with AI and hardware? The possibilities are endless! You are free to choose your hardware, AI models, and deployment methods. There are no fixed competition tracks or restrictions on project direction. Here are eight areas to inspire your creativity: Vision Recognition Voice and Sound Environment and Smart Home Robotics and Control Edge AI / TinyML Wearables and Assistive Devices LLMs and Physical Interaction Creative Projects and Education These ideas are only starting points, not limitations. You can explore unconventional applications, combine multiple technologies, or develop an entirely different AI hardware concept. We encourage original thinking and creative approaches. Develop and complete a working physical prototype. Document your design, implementation, and demonstration process. Publish and Submit Your Project Once your project is ready<dynamic-value> it with the community. Publish a complete project report on a public platform. Unlock Color PCB Printing with PCBWay! by: PCBWay Mar 08,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Color PCB Printing PCBWay Service Nowadays, traditional PCB printing technology can no longer meet the aesthetic requirements of modern circuit board production. To better fulfill customers' design needs, we are pleased to announce that PCBWay has introduced UV printing equipment. This equipment utilizes UV-curable inks to achieve high-quality image printing on various materials, including fiberglass boards, metal substrates, ceramic substrates, flexible boards, and rigid-flex boards. Entrance https://www.pcbway.com/orderonline.aspx Prerequisites for Ordering Maximum size for a single piece: 270*470MM; Selection of background soldermask color required. Design Specifications Drill holes, traces, soldermasks, and outline designs must comply with specifications. Avoid placing colored characters in areas with solder mask openings, such as surface-mount pads or through-hole pads. What kind of files should be provided for color printing? Method One : Draw colored characters on the silkscreen layer of the Gerber and provide reference pictures. For example: Method Two : If you include information about colored silkscreen in the Gerber layer, each individual color must have its own layer. If there is only one layer, we can only print one color. [This method is not recommended] . If you need to print in multiple colors, we recommend using method One and providing us with a reference picture. 4.Please send the images you want to print on the PCB in the following formats: AI, PDF, JPEG, PNG, TIFF, etc., and indicate your desired printing location on the board. 5.If the image contains a QR code, please ensure that the QR code can be accurately scanned and recognized. Note : If you choose UV printing Multi-color, we will use matte UV color printing by default. When designing the colored characters on the bottom layer, be careful not to design the colored characters as mirrored inverses. (The process of color printing is different from that of standard PCB silkscreen printing. When printing colorful characters on the bottom layer, they are printed with the bottom layer of the PCB facing up.) For situations where the entire top or bottom side requires full-color printing, regardless of the solder mask color you choose, we will use a white solder mask on the full-color printed side and then proceed with the color printing. This is for a better printing effect. Please upload the print image, positioning image, and Gerber in one compressed file. By providing a clear positioning image and necessary instructions, you can assist PCBWay in accurately determining and achieving the desired printing position. Matte UV Color Printing vs. Glossy UV Color Printing Matte ink does not increase the overall thickness, and the PCB's appearance looks smooth. Glossy ink increases the overall thickness and may affect the soldering of component pads. The appearance is beautiful but uneven. Features Adopting UV-LED lamp curing, which enables instant drying, can significantly enhances production efficiency. UV printing technology employs UV-curable inks, ensuring firm and clear printing information resistant to fading, thus enhancing product identification and aesthetics. The normal print survives SMT reflow. Since it's ink, there will be some discoloration. UV printing technology can present images in various colors and styles, meeting customers' personalized requirements. Professional industrial-grade UV printers support high-precision printing, delivering exquisite results whether on flat panels or rolled materials. Unlike traditional printing methods, UV printing does not produce volatile organic compounds during the production process, ensuring air quality in the production workshop and providing employees with a safer and healthier working environment. FAQ on UV Printing: Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with water? Yes, it can be cleaned with water. Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with alcohol? It is more difficult to clean after being exposed to alcohol and baked (currently, the board undergoes a short baking process after UV printing). However, with increased contact time with alcohol and vigorous scrubbing, it can be removed. This also depends on whether the UV is on the copper surface or the solder mask surface. How hard is the UV printed surface (sensitivity to scratches)? The UV surface is not sensitive to scratches. However, compared to the solder mask, it is less scratch-resistant because UV printing is ink that is sprayed on and is relatively thin. Welcome to give it a try if you're interested! Besides, PCBWay will continue to enhance its manufacturing capabilities to bring more choices and personalized services to customers in the future. Verify Now Blog > 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement by: Mila Oct 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout PCB Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines PCB Design Guidelines PCB layout involves more than simply placing components and routing traces. Component spacing, decoupling capacitor placement, pad connections, thermal management, and manufacturing constraints all affect PCB assembly quality and long-term reliability. The following PCB layout guidelines cover 12 practical details that engineers should consider during PCB component placement and design. 1. SMT Component Spacing The spacing between surface-mount technology (SMT) components is an important consideration in PCB layout. Insufficient spacing can make solder paste printing and component placement more difficult, increase the risk of solder bridging, and complicate rework and maintenance. The following values can serve as preliminary references for PCB component spacing: Same-type components: A spacing of at least 0.3 mm may be used as a reference. Different types of components: A spacing of at least 0.13 × h + 0.3 mm may be used as a reference, where h is the maximum height difference between adjacent components. Components requiring manual placement or rework: A spacing of at least 1.5 mm may be considered, depending on the available working space and tools. These values are for reference only and are not universal manufacturing standards. Actual PCB component spacing should be determined based on component packages, pad dimensions, solder paste printing, placement equipment, and the manufacturing and assembly capabilities of the PCB supplier. 2. Spacing Between Through-Hole and SMT Components Adequate spacing should also be maintained between through-hole components and SMT components to prevent interference during component placement, soldering, and subsequent rework. A spacing of 1–3 mm can serve as a general reference, but the actual distance depends on component dimensions, lead positions, soldering methods, and maintenance requirements. For PCBs assembled using wave soldering, engineers should also consider component orientation, shadowing effects caused by adjacent components, and whether solder can reach the joints effectively. 3. IC Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to the corresponding IC power pins. This helps shorten the current loop between the power supply and ground, reducing parasitic inductance and power supply noise. When an IC has multiple power pins, the number, capacitance, and placement of decoupling capacitors should be determined according to the datasheet, power distribution network, and actual current requirements. Where individual power pins require dedicated decoupling, the corresponding capacitors should be placed as close to those pins as possible. The grounding path is equally important. Keep the connections between the power pin, decoupling capacitor, and ground as short as practical. Unnecessarily long traces or excessive vias can reduce decoupling effectiveness, particularly at high frequencies. 4. Component Orientation and Clearance Near PCB Edges PCBs often undergo routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes. Components near PCB edges therefore require special attention to their orientation and clearance. First, consider the mechanical stress generated during depanelization. Ceramic capacitors, connectors, and other mechanically sensitive components should be positioned to minimize stress concentration at solder joints and component bodies. Component orientation should be determined by the depanelization method, pad geometry, and component characteristics rather than by a universal rule that all components must be parallel to the cutting direction. Second, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near PCB edges to prevent damage from cutting tools or depanelization equipment. The required clearance depends on the depanelization method, such as V-scoring, routing, or mouse bites, as well as component dimensions and the PCB manufacturer's capabilities. For components that are particularly sensitive to mechanical stress, consider using a depanelization method that reduces stress on the board and solder joints. 5. Connecting Adjacent PCB Pads When adjacent pads must be connected to the same net, the copper connections and trace widths should be planned carefully. Poorly designed copper connections may reduce the effective clearance between pads and increase the risk of solder bridging. During PCB layout, maintain adequate electrical clearance between pads and select trace widths according to current-carrying requirements. For fine-pitch components, pay particular attention to the relationship between pads, traces, and solder mask openings to avoid problems with solder paste printing and soldering quality. After completing the layout, run design rule checks (DRC) and verify that the design meets the PCB manufacturer's fabrication and assembly requirements. 6. Thermal Relief vs. Solid Copper Connections When a pad is connected to a copper plane, the connection method should be selected based on soldering requirements, current-carrying capacity, and thermal performance. Two common methods are thermal relief connections and solid copper connections. A thermal relief connection uses several narrow copper spokes to connect the pad to the surrounding copper plane. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Using Teardrops in PCB Layout When a trace connects to a pad or via through a narrow junction, a teardrop can be added where appropriate to create a smoother transition between the trace and the connection point. Teardrops offer several potential benefits: Improved connection reliability: They increase the copper area at the trace-to-pad junction, helping reduce the risk of a weakened or broken connection caused by drill misalignment, manufacturing tolerances, or mechanical stress. Enhanced mechanical robustness: The wider transition can make the connection less vulnerable to local narrowing or separation. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Verify Now Blog > 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement by: Mila Oct 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout PCB Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines PCB Design Guidelines PCB layout involves more than simply placing components and routing traces. Component spacing, decoupling capacitor placement, pad connections, thermal management, and manufacturing constraints all affect PCB assembly quality and long-term reliability. The following PCB layout guidelines cover 12 practical details that engineers should consider during PCB component placement and design. 1. SMT Component Spacing The spacing between surface-mount technology (SMT) components is an important consideration in PCB layout. Insufficient spacing can make solder paste printing and component placement more difficult, increase the risk of solder bridging, and complicate rework and maintenance. The following values can serve as preliminary references for PCB component spacing: Same-type components: A spacing of at least 0.3 mm may be used as a reference. Different types of components: A spacing of at least 0.13 × h + 0.3 mm may be used as a reference, where h is the maximum height difference between adjacent components. Components requiring manual placement or rework: A spacing of at least 1.5 mm may be considered, depending on the available working space and tools. These values are for reference only and are not universal manufacturing standards. Actual PCB component spacing should be determined based on component packages, pad dimensions, solder paste printing, placement equipment, and the manufacturing and assembly capabilities of the PCB supplier. 2. Spacing Between Through-Hole and SMT Components Adequate spacing should also be maintained between through-hole components and SMT components to prevent interference during component placement, soldering, and subsequent rework. A spacing of 1–3 mm can serve as a general reference, but the actual distance depends on component dimensions, lead positions, soldering methods, and maintenance requirements. For PCBs assembled using wave soldering, engineers should also consider component orientation, shadowing effects caused by adjacent components, and whether solder can reach the joints effectively. 3. IC Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to the corresponding IC power pins. This helps shorten the current loop between the power supply and ground, reducing parasitic inductance and power supply noise. When an IC has multiple power pins, the number, capacitance, and placement of decoupling capacitors should be determined according to the datasheet, power distribution network, and actual current requirements. Where individual power pins require dedicated decoupling, the corresponding capacitors should be placed as close to those pins as possible. The grounding path is equally important. Keep the connections between the power pin, decoupling capacitor, and ground as short as practical. Unnecessarily long traces or excessive vias can reduce decoupling effectiveness, particularly at high frequencies. 4. Component Orientation and Clearance Near PCB Edges PCBs often undergo routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes. Components near PCB edges therefore require special attention to their orientation and clearance. First, consider the mechanical stress generated during depanelization. Ceramic capacitors, connectors, and other mechanically sensitive components should be positioned to minimize stress concentration at solder joints and component bodies. Component orientation should be determined by the depanelization method, pad geometry, and component characteristics rather than by a universal rule that all components must be parallel to the cutting direction. Second, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near PCB edges to prevent damage from cutting tools or depanelization equipment. The required clearance depends on the depanelization method, such as V-scoring, routing, or mouse bites, as well as component dimensions and the PCB manufacturer's capabilities. For components that are particularly sensitive to mechanical stress, consider using a depanelization method that reduces stress on the board and solder joints. 5. Connecting Adjacent PCB Pads When adjacent pads must be connected to the same net, the copper connections and trace widths should be planned carefully. Poorly designed copper connections may reduce the effective clearance between pads and increase the risk of solder bridging. During PCB layout, maintain adequate electrical clearance between pads and select trace widths according to current-carrying requirements. For fine-pitch components, pay particular attention to the relationship between pads, traces, and solder mask openings to avoid problems with solder paste printing and soldering quality. After completing the layout, run design rule checks (DRC) and verify that the design meets the PCB manufacturer's fabrication and assembly requirements. 6. Thermal Relief vs. Solid Copper Connections When a pad is connected to a copper plane, the connection method should be selected based on soldering requirements, current-carrying capacity, and thermal performance. Two common methods are thermal relief connections and solid copper connections. A thermal relief connection uses several narrow copper spokes to connect the pad to the surrounding copper plane. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Using Teardrops in PCB Layout When a trace connects to a pad or via through a narrow junction, a teardrop can be added where appropriate to create a smoother transition between the trace and the connection point. Teardrops offer several potential benefits: Improved connection reliability: They increase the copper area at the trace-to-pad junction, helping reduce the risk of a weakened or broken connection caused by drill misalignment, manufacturing tolerances, or mechanical stress. Enhanced mechanical robustness: The wider transition can make the connection less vulnerable to local narrowing or separation. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Avoid unnecessary abrupt changes in trace width near pad connections. 9. Handling Unused IC Pins Unused IC pins must be handled according to the device datasheet and application requirements. They should not all be connected to ground or left floating indiscriminately. For example: NC pins: Follow the datasheet instructions. Some pins must remain unconnected and should not be grounded without authorization. Unused input pins: Connect them to the specified logic level or use the recommended pull-up, pull-down, or other biasing method to prevent undefined input states. Unused output pins: Do not connect them directly to ground or a power rail unless the datasheet explicitly permits it. Pins permitted to float: Leave them unconnected only when this is allowed or required by the device documentation. For physical pins that are present on the IC but not used in the application, ensure that the PCB footprint correctly represents the actual package. Whether the corresponding pads should be connected to ground or handled in another way depends on the pin function and the device manufacturer's recommendations. Adding a pad and connecting it to ground does not necessarily provide effective shielding. An incorrect connection may instead cause a short circuit or interfere with normal device operation. 10. Via-in-Pad Design Considerations During PCB layout, placing a conventional open via directly within a pad can cause solder to flow into the hole during assembly. This may result in insufficient solder at the joint, poor soldering quality, or other assembly defects. For ordinary SMT pads, avoid placing untreated open vias directly within the pads, particularly for fine-pitch components, unless the manufacturing process supports the design. However, vias are not universally prohibited within pads. Via-in-pad is a common design approach for packages such as BGAs, where routing density and electrical performance may require it. Depending on the application, via filling, capping, or other appropriate via treatments may be needed to prevent solder loss and ensure reliable assembly. Select the appropriate approach based on the component package, via structure, and PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. 11. PCB Edge Clearance for Traces, Pads, and Components Copper traces, pads, and components should maintain adequate clearance from PCB edges to prevent damage during fabrication, depanelization, and subsequent assembly. If copper features or pads are too close to the board edge, routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes may damage the copper, expose conductors, or compromise electrical reliability. For single-sided boards and substrates with relatively low mechanical strength, additional attention should be paid to structural integrity and component placement near the edges. The required PCB edge clearance should be determined according to the board material, thickness, depanelization method, and manufacturer's capabilities. Include these clearances in the PCB design rules and verify them before manufacturing. 12. Keep Electrolytic Capacitors Away from Heat Sources Electrolytic capacitors are sensitive to operating temperature. Prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures can accelerate electrolyte loss and shorten capacitor service life. During PCB layout, avoid placing electrolytic capacitors too close to power resistors, power semiconductors, transformers, or other heat-generating components whenever possible. If close placement is unavoidable, evaluate the thermal impact based on component temperature rise, airflow direction, and the actual operating environment. Also consider the capacitor's rated operating temperature, ripple current, and self-heating to ensure that it operates within acceptable limits under real-world conditions. Distance from a heat source alone is not sufficient to determine whether a capacitor is safe. Thermal design and the operating conditions of the complete product must also be considered. Conclusion PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also manufacturability, soldering quality, and long-term reliability. In addition to routing and component placement, engineers should consider assembly processes, mechanical stress, thermal requirements, and the recommendations provided in component datasheets. After completing the PCB design, perform design rule checks and verify the layout against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities and assembly requirements. Careful attention to these PCB layout guidelines can help reduce design issues and improve PCB fabrication and assembly reliability Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout by: Mila Nov 06,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout clock circuit crystal oscillator pcb Layout pcb clock signal routing Clock circuits play an essential role in electronic systems by providing timing signals that synchronize the operation of different components. However, improper clock circuit design can lead to signal interference, timing errors, and system instability. This article explores the PCB design guidelines for crystal circuits, active oscillators, and clock distributors, covering key considerations for component placement, signal routing, and noise reduction. 1. Crystal A clock is an essential part of any electronic system. It acts like the heartbeat of the system, providing synchronization signals to different components. If the clock signal becomes unstable or fails, the entire system may malfunction or stop working. Therefore, proper clock circuit design is essential in PCB design. Common clock sources and distribution components used in PCBs include crystals, oscillators, and clock distributors. Some ICs may generate their own clock signals internally. However, the clock signal ultimately originates from a crystal, an oscillator, or another clock source before being distributed to other components. When designing a crystal circuit, consider the following guidelines: Place the crystal as close as possible to the IC's oscillator pins to minimize trace length and reduce external interference. For designs with high electromagnetic compatibility requirements, consider using a crystal with a metal shield package. Ensure that the shield is properly grounded according to the component datasheet. Avoid routing other signal traces beneath the crystal and its load capacitors, especially high-speed digital signals. A continuous GND reference plane can be provided beneath the crystal circuit according to the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations. Keep high-speed digital signal traces away from the crystal to reduce crosstalk. Keep the ground connections of the load capacitors as short as possible to minimize parasitic inductance and provide a low-impedance return path. A GND guard area can be added around the crystal according to the recommended layout. If necessary, use GND vias to connect the ground copper on different layers. Place the crystal and its two load capacitors close to the IC's oscillator pins. Follow the component manufacturer's reference design for the exact placement arrangement. Common crystal packages used in PCB design include 2-pin through-hole packages, 2-pin SMD packages, and 4-pin SMD packages. （Common crystal package types） Although crystals are available in different package sizes and specifications, their basic operating principles and peripheral circuit designs are similar. Therefore, many PCB placement and routing guidelines are applicable across different crystal designs. A basic crystal circuit is shown below: （Basic crystal circuit schematic） The two capacitors shown in the schematic are load capacitors. They connect the two crystal terminals to ground and provide the required load capacitance for stable oscillation. Their values should be determined based on the crystal datasheet, the IC's internal oscillator characteristics, and the parasitic capacitance of the PCB. 2. Crystal Circuit Placement and Routing When placing a crystal circuit, position the two load capacitors as close as possible to the crystal and the IC's oscillator pins. This helps minimize trace length and reduce the impact of parasitic parameters. The placement is shown below: （Crystal circuit placement） When routing the crystal circuit, keep the two connections between the crystal and the IC as short as possible and preferably close to each other to reduce parasitic capacitance and external interference. Note that these two traces are not true differential signal lines, so differential routing rules should not be applied directly. Avoid unnecessary vias and follow the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations to determine whether GND guard traces are needed. The routing layout is shown below: （Crystal circuit routing） 3. Crystal Circuit Design Variations The circuit described above is the most basic and commonly used crystal circuit design. In practical PCB designs, additional components such as series resistors and test points may be included to meet debugging or signal integrity requirements. However, the basic design principles remain the same. Based on the guidelines above, consider the following points when placing components: （Crystal circuit layout with a series resistor and test point） Place the crystal, associated capacitors, and series resistor on the same PCB layer whenever possible to reduce vias and shorten connection paths. If test points are required, avoid long stubs. Additional trace branches may introduce parasitic capacitance and affect oscillator stability. Avoid placing high-power components near the crystal, such as power ICs, MOSFETs, and inductors, as heat generated by these components may affect crystal frequency stability. Routing guidelines: Place and route the crystal on the same layer as the IC whenever possible to minimize vias. If layer changes are necessary, ensure a continuous return path and add nearby GND vias when needed. Keep crystal traces as short as possible. Trace width should be determined based on the IC manufacturer's recommendations and PCB fabrication capabilities rather than increased unnecessarily. GND guard traces can be added around the crystal circuit when appropriate. Connect them to the reference ground plane using GND vias. Keep the crystal circuit area relatively isolated. Avoid routing other high-speed signals through this area to reduce crosstalk and external noise interference. 4. Oscillator Circuit Design Unlike passive crystals, active oscillators integrate an internal oscillation circuit and can directly output clock signals. An active oscillator circuit typically consists of an oscillator device, a power supply decoupling circuit, and an optional source-series resistor selected according to the output interface and load requirements. A typical oscillator circuit is shown below: （Active oscillator circuit schematic） The PCB placement and routing layout is shown below: （Active oscillator PCB layout and routing） Placement and routing guidelines: Place power decoupling capacitors as close as possible to the oscillator's power supply pins. Prioritize a short power and ground loop for the high-frequency decoupling capacitor. If multiple decoupling capacitors are used, select their capacitance values and placement based on the component datasheet and power integrity requirements. There is no need to mechanically follow a fixed large-to-small capacitor arrangement. Determine whether a source-series resistor is needed based on the oscillator's output type, drive capability, trace length, and load conditions. If required, place it as close as possible to the oscillator output pin. Determine the clock signal impedance based on the oscillator output interface, receiver requirements, and PCB stackup. For clock signals that require transmission line control, implement appropriate impedance design. For long clock traces, consider routing them on an inner layer while maintaining a continuous reference plane. If layer transitions are necessary, add nearby GND return vias when appropriate. Maintain adequate spacing between clock traces and other signal traces to reduce crosstalk. The required spacing depends on signal edge rate, trace length, and layer-to-layer coupling. For longer clock traces, GND guard traces may be used when appropriate. Ensure that the guard traces are properly grounded and do not compromise signal integrity. 5. Clock Distributor Design A clock distributor is primarily used to distribute a clock signal from a clock source to multiple ICs or functional modules. Different clock distributors vary in terms of output count, frequency range, output interface, and drive capability. During PCB design, carefully plan the placement of the clock distributor relative to the receiving ICs to minimize clock signal routing distances. For designs that require clock skew control, also consider the routing lengths and loads of different output channels. The clock distributor is often placed at a relatively central position among the receiving devices. A typical clock distributor circuit is shown below: （Clock distributor circuit schematic） The PCB layout is shown below: （Clock distributor PCB layout） Placement and routing guidelines: Place the clock generation circuit as close as possible to the clock distributor. Common clock sources include crystals, active oscillators, and other clock generation circuits. Position the clock distributor appropriately in relation to the receiving ICs to minimize clock signal routing distances. For designs requiring clock skew control, keep the routing lengths and loads of related clock output paths as consistent as possible. Avoid placing high-power components near the clock distributor, such as power ICs, MOSFETs, and inductors, as temperature variations may affect clock performance. For long clock signal traces, consider routing them on inner layers while maintaining a continuous reference plane. If layer transitions are necessary, add GND return vias close to the signal vias to provide a continuous return path. Control trace impedance and signal spacing according to the clock frequency, edge rate, and interface requirements to reduce crosstalk and signal reflections. A well-designed clock circuit is essential for maintaining stable and reliable operation in electronic systems. Whether using a crystal, an active oscillator, or a clock distributor, careful component placement, short signal paths, proper grounding, and appropriate impedance control all contribute to better clock signal integrity. By following these PCB clock circuit design guidelines, engineers can reduce noise interference, minimize signal distortion, and improve overall system stability. Verify Now Blog > Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid by: Mila Nov 04,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Differential Pair Differential Pair Routing High-Speed PCB Design Differential Pair Routing In high-speed PCB design , differential pairs are increasingly used, especially in high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe. These interfaces commonly use differential signaling for reliable data transmission. Why is differential signaling so widely used? Compared with conventional single-ended routing, differential pairs offer better noise immunity, help suppress common-mode noise and electromagnetic interference (EMI), and improve signal integrity and timing performance. Differential Pair Routing Requirements In PCB design, a differential pair consists of two closely coupled signal traces. To ensure signal transmission quality, these traces generally need to have matched lengths, equal widths, consistent spacing, and symmetrical routing. Differential impedance must also be controlled according to the design requirements. （Differential Pair Routing Requirements） 1. Equal Length Equal length means keeping the two traces in a differential pair as close in length as possible. Verify Now Blog > Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid by: Mila Nov 04,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Differential Pair Differential Pair Routing High-Speed PCB Design Differential Pair Routing In high-speed PCB design , differential pairs are increasingly used, especially in high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe. These interfaces commonly use differential signaling for reliable data transmission. Why is differential signaling so widely used? Compared with conventional single-ended routing, differential pairs offer better noise immunity, help suppress common-mode noise and electromagnetic interference (EMI), and improve signal integrity and timing performance. Differential Pair Routing Requirements In PCB design, a differential pair consists of two closely coupled signal traces. To ensure signal transmission quality, these traces generally need to have matched lengths, equal widths, consistent spacing, and symmetrical routing. Differential impedance must also be controlled according to the design requirements. （Differential Pair Routing Requirements） 1. Equal Length Equal length means keeping the two traces in a differential pair as close in length as possible. The purpose is to control the propagation delay difference (skew) between the two signals, maintain proper timing alignment, and reduce signal imbalance and the resulting common-mode noise. 2. Equal Width and Spacing Equal width means maintaining the same trace width for both signals. Equal spacing means keeping the distance between the two traces as consistent as possible, allowing them to run symmetrically and in parallel. This helps maintain a stable coupling relationship between the two traces, minimizes differential impedance variations, and improves signal transmission quality. 3. Controlled Differential Impedance When designing a PCB with differential pairs, one of the first steps is to determine the target differential impedance required by the interface and plan the routing accordingly. It is also important to minimize impedance variations along the routing path. Differential impedance is affected by several factors, including trace width, spacing between the two traces, copper thickness, PCB material, and stackup structure. These factors should all be considered during the design process to maintain consistent differential impedance. 4. Maintain a Continuous Reference Plane Although differential signals offer strong noise immunity, they still require an appropriate reference plane. The reference plane beneath the differential pair should remain continuous whenever possible. Avoid routing differential pairs across split ground planes or slots in the reference plane, as these discontinuities can alter return paths and cause impedance variations. Common Misconceptions About Differential Pair Routing Misconception 1: Differential Signals Do Not Need a Ground Plane as a Return Path, or the Two Traces Can Serve as Each Other's Return Paths. Differential signals offer strong immunity to common-mode noise, but this does not mean they do not need a reference plane. In fact, the return-current path depends on the coupling between the two differential traces and their coupling to the reference plane. Differential-mode return current is primarily associated with the electromagnetic coupling between the two traces, while the reference plane still affects the return path and impedance characteristics, especially for common-mode currents. When the reference plane contains splits or slots, the return-current path may change, causing impedance discontinuities, signal degradation, and increased EMI. Therefore, differential pairs should be routed over a continuous reference plane whenever possible, avoiding split ground regions. In addition, removing the reference plane beneath differential traces to suppress common-mode noise is not recommended. This can make impedance control more difficult and disrupt the return path for common-mode currents, potentially increasing electromagnetic radiation. （Differential Signal Reference Plane） Misconception 2: Maintaining Consistent Spacing Is More Important Than Matching Trace Lengths. In practical PCB routing, it is not always possible to satisfy every differential pair design requirement simultaneously. Component pin placement, via locations, and available routing space may require designers to introduce serpentine routing to match trace lengths. However, this can cause some sections of the differential pair to lose their parallel alignment or consistent spacing. In such cases, design priorities should be determined according to the interface specifications and application requirements. For high-speed differential interfaces with strict intra-pair skew limits, length matching is particularly important. However, trace spacing also affects coupling and differential impedance, so it should not be overlooked. During routing, priority should be given to meeting interface timing and impedance requirements. Symmetry, consistent spacing, and routing continuity should then be maintained as much as possible, rather than focusing on just one routing parameter. （Differential Line Length Matching） Misconception 3: Differential Traces Must Always Be Routed Close Together. Routing differential traces close together strengthens the coupling between them, improving noise immunity and helping reduce electromagnetic radiation through partial magnetic field cancellation. However, closer spacing is not always better. The spacing should be determined by the target differential impedance, PCB stackup, and application requirements. Excessively small spacing may make impedance control and manufacturing more challenging. To reduce crosstalk, maintain sufficient spacing between differential pairs and other signal traces. The 4W rule (spacing of at least four times the trace width) can serve as an initial guideline, but actual spacing should be determined by the design requirements. Ground guard traces connected to the reference plane through stitching vias can also provide additional isolation. For high-frequency applications, coplanar waveguide (CPW) structures are another option for controlling differential impedance. （Differential Line Spacing） Conclusion Differential pair routing is an important part of high-speed PCB design . In addition to trace length, width, and spacing, designers must also consider differential impedance, reference-plane continuity, and interference from surrounding signals. Only by considering all these factors together can designers ensure reliable differential signal transmission and improve overall PCB performance and reliability. Verify Now Blog > How Does a Thermistor Circuit Work? NTC, PTC, and PCB Layout How Does a Thermistor Circuit Work? NTC, PTC, and PCB Layout by: Mila Nov 18,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout thermistor circuit NTC thermistor PTC thermistor NTC vs PTC thermistor thermistor pcb Temperature monitoring is essential for protecting electronic components, maintaining system stability, and ensuring reliable operation. Whether preventing a battery from overheating or keeping an industrial motor within its operating temperature range, accurate temperature sensing plays an important role. Among various temperature sensors, thermistors are widely used because of their simple structure, low cost, and fast response. This article explains how thermistors work, explores common measurement circuits, discusses key performance parameters, and compares NTC and PTC thermistors to help guide component selection and PCB design . 1. What Is a Thermistor? Understanding How It Works Working Principle: A thermistor is a resistor whose resistance changes significantly with temperature. The name comes from the combination of "thermal" and "resistor." Its key characteristic is that its resistance varies in response to changes in its own temperature. This property allows a thermistor to convert temperature, a physical quantity, into a change in electrical resistance, which can then be converted into a measurable voltage signal through an external circuit. Figure 1. Different types of thermistors Two Main Types: Based on how their resistance changes with temperature, thermistors are generally divided into two categories: NTC (Negative Temperature Coefficient) Thermistors: Their resistance decreases as temperature increases. NTC thermistors are among the most widely used temperature-sensing components due to their low cost and high sensitivity. Common applications include battery temperature monitoring, power management, and household appliance temperature control. PTC (Positive Temperature Coefficient) Thermistors: Their resistance increases as temperature rises. Depending on their materials and resistance characteristics, PTC thermistors can be further divided into two types: Nonlinear (Switching-Type) PTC Thermistors: Their resistance increases sharply near a specific temperature, known as the Curie temperature. They are commonly used for overcurrent protection, overtemperature protection, and resettable fuses. Linear PTC Thermistors: Typically made from silicon, these devices have a relatively stable positive temperature coefficient. Their resistance increases approximately linearly with temperature, making them suitable for temperature measurement applications. Simply put, an NTC thermistor behaves like a component that offers less resistance as it gets hotter. A linear PTC thermistor works in the opposite way: its resistance increases with temperature, generally in a more uniform and predictable manner. 2. How to Read a Thermistor: Two Common Measurement Circuits A thermistor does not generate an electrical signal on its own. It requires an external excitation source to convert its resistance changes into a measurable voltage signal. The following are two commonly used measurement circuits. Voltage Divider Circuit (Constant-Voltage Excitation) Figure 2. Thermistor in a voltage divider configuration This is one of the simplest and most cost-effective thermistor measurement methods. A thermistor is connected in series with a fixed reference resistor and supplied by a stable voltage source, such as VCC. By measuring the voltage across one of the resistors, the temperature information can be obtained. Working Principle: When the temperature changes, the thermistor's resistance changes accordingly. According to the voltage divider principle, the output voltage, V_TEMP, also changes. By measuring this voltage, the thermistor resistance can be calculated, and the corresponding temperature can then be determined. Advantages: The circuit is simple, requires few components, and has a low implementation cost, making it suitable for many conventional temperature-sensing applications. Considerations: Variations in the supply voltage VCC can affect V_TEMP and introduce measurement errors. To reduce this effect, a ratiometric measurement method can be used. For example, the same voltage source can serve as both the excitation voltage for the divider and the ADC reference voltage. This helps cancel out the effects of supply voltage fluctuations. Constant-Current Excitation Circuit Figure 3. Thermistor measurement using constant-current excitation Another approach is to use a precision constant-current source (I BIAS ) to supply a stable current to the thermistor. Working Principle: According to Ohm's law, V = I × R. Since the current flowing through the thermistor remains constant, the voltage across it, V_TEMP, is proportional to its resistance: V TEMP = I BIAS × R THERMISTOR When the temperature changes and the thermistor resistance varies, the output voltage changes accordingly. Advantages: Within the operating range of the current source, the output voltage is linearly proportional to the thermistor resistance. This makes resistance measurement and signal processing more straightforward, especially in applications requiring relatively high measurement accuracy. Considerations: The accuracy, temperature drift, and output voltage range of the current source all affect measurement results. In addition, excessive excitation current can cause thermistor self-heating. Therefore, the bias current must be selected carefully. The Next Step: Signal Processing The resulting analog voltage signal, V TEMP , is typically sent to an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) input on a microcontroller (MCU) for digital processing. Alternatively, it can be sent to a voltage comparator and compared with a preset threshold voltage to implement a basic overtemperature alarm. Figure 4. Overtemperature threshold detection using a thermistor and comparator 3. Key Parameters for Improving Thermistor Performance and Accuracy When selecting a thermistor, its nominal resistance is not the only parameter to consider. The following characteristics also play an important role in determining temperature measurement accuracy, stability, and overall circuit complexity. Resistance Tolerance Resistance tolerance refers to the allowable deviation between a thermistor's actual resistance and its nominal resistance at a specified temperature, typically 25°C. For example, a tolerance of ±1% means the actual resistance can vary within 1% of the specified nominal value at that temperature. NTC Thermistors: The resistance tolerance of an NTC thermistor depends not only on its nominal resistance at 25°C but also on the tolerance of its B-value and other material characteristics. Therefore, even if an NTC thermistor has a resistance tolerance of ±1% at 25°C, its actual measurement error may increase significantly at other temperatures. Linear PTC Thermistors: Some silicon-based linear PTC thermistors maintain relatively stable resistance-temperature characteristics over a wide operating temperature range, helping achieve consistent measurements. However, their actual tolerance still depends on the specific device and its datasheet specifications. Temperature Sensitivity and Measurement Resolution Sensitivity describes how much a thermistor's resistance changes in response to a change in temperature. It reflects the sensor's ability to respond to temperature variations. Measurement resolution, on the other hand, refers to the smallest temperature change that the entire measurement system can detect. NTC Thermistors: The resistance-temperature relationship of an NTC thermistor is nonlinear, and its sensitivity varies with temperature. It generally has higher relative sensitivity at lower temperatures, while its relative sensitivity tends to decrease as temperature rises. Linear PTC Thermistors: Silicon-based linear PTC thermistors typically exhibit a more uniform resistance change with temperature, helping maintain a consistent measurement response across a relatively wide temperature range. It is important to note that the final measurement resolution depends not only on the thermistor itself but also on the ADC resolution, reference voltage, signal noise, and external circuit design. Linearization: Simplifying Circuit Design Ideally, a sensor's output signal should have a linear relationship with the measured temperature. This simplifies subsequent data processing and temperature conversion. Challenges with NTC Thermistors: The resistance-temperature (R-T) relationship of an NTC thermistor is strongly nonlinear. To improve measurement linearity over the operating temperature range, software compensation is commonly used. Alternatively, additional components, such as a parallel resistor, can be added to the circuit for hardware linearization. Both approaches introduce some additional design or computational complexity. Figure 5. Improving the linearity of an NTC measurement circuit by adding a parallel resistor Advantages of Linear PTC Thermistors: Silicon-based linear PTC thermistors have an inherently more linear R-T characteristic, which can reduce the need for nonlinear compensation and simplify temperature conversion. However, the actual linearity of the output voltage relative to temperature also depends on the excitation circuit design. Figure 6. Linear PTC thermistors do not require a parallel resistor Self-Heating and Long-Term Drift Self-Heating: When current flows through a thermistor, Joule heating occurs, causing the device's own temperature to rise above the surrounding ambient temperature. This can introduce errors into temperature measurements. The degree of self-heating depends on the excitation method and the device's thermal dissipation conditions. For example, under constant-current excitation, thermistor power dissipation is: P = I² × R For an NTC thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature rises, so its power dissipation also decreases under constant-current excitation. Under constant-voltage excitation, however, power dissipation is: P = V² / R In this case, a decrease in NTC resistance may cause power dissipation to increase. Therefore, the excitation current or voltage should be properly controlled to prevent self-heating from affecting measurement accuracy. Long-Term Drift: Long-term drift refers to changes in a thermistor's resistance-temperature characteristics after prolonged operation or exposure to environmental factors such as temperature and humidity. It is closely related to the material, manufacturing process, operating temperature, and application environment. When selecting a thermistor, check the long-term stability and aging test data provided in its datasheet. This is particularly important in applications with demanding reliability requirements, such as automotive electronics and industrial control systems. Calibration All temperature sensors may exhibit component-to-component variations and system-level errors. Therefore, calibration is often necessary in applications requiring high measurement accuracy. NTC Thermistors: Because of their nonlinear R-T characteristics and potentially varying resistance errors across different temperatures, two-point or multipoint calibration may be required in applications with a wide temperature range or strict accuracy requirements. Linear PTC Thermistors: Thanks to their relatively linear characteristics, some devices can achieve good measurement accuracy with single-point calibration. However, multipoint calibration may still be necessary when high accuracy is required across the entire operating temperature range. The appropriate calibration method should be determined based on the required accuracy, operating temperature range, and device datasheet. 4. Software Processing: Converting Voltage into Temperature After the MCU reads the ADC value corresponding to V_TEMP, an algorithm is needed to convert it into an actual temperature value. Two common methods are used. Lookup Table Method A lookup table is created in advance to establish the relationship between resistance or ADC values and temperature. The MCU searches the table using the measured value to obtain the corresponding temperature. Interpolation can also be used to improve conversion accuracy. This method offers fast execution and simple implementation, but it requires additional memory. It is a practical option for MCUs with limited computational resources. Equation-Based Calculation Mathematical models are used to fit the thermistor's R-T curve and convert the measured resistance into temperature. For NTC Thermistors: The Steinhart-Hart equation is commonly used: 1/T = A + B*ln(R) + C*[ln(R)]³ Where T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin (K), R is the thermistor resistance, and A, B, and C are coefficients determined by the device's characteristics. For Linear PTC Thermistors: If the device has a sufficiently linear resistance-temperature relationship, a simple linear equation can be used: T = T₀ + (R − R₀) / (α × R₀) Where T₀ is the reference temperature, R₀ is the resistance at that temperature, and α is the temperature coefficient. For applications requiring higher accuracy, polynomial fitting or lookup tables can also be used to compensate for deviations from ideal linearity. 5. The name comes from the combination of "thermal" and "resistor." Its key characteristic is that its resistance varies in response to changes in its own temperature. This property allows a thermistor to convert temperature, a physical quantity, into a change in electrical resistance, which can then be converted into a measurable voltage signal through an external circuit. Figure 1. Different types of thermistors Two Main Types: Based on how their resistance changes with temperature, thermistors are generally divided into two categories: NTC (Negative Temperature Coefficient) Thermistors: Their resistance decreases as temperature increases. NTC thermistors are among the most widely used temperature-sensing components due to their low cost and high sensitivity. Common applications include battery temperature monitoring, power management, and household appliance temperature control. PTC (Positive Temperature Coefficient) Thermistors: Their resistance increases as temperature rises. Depending on their materials and resistance characteristics, PTC thermistors can be further divided into two types: Nonlinear (Switching-Type) PTC Thermistors: Their resistance increases sharply near a specific temperature, known as the Curie temperature. They are commonly used for overcurrent protection, overtemperature protection, and resettable fuses. Linear PTC Thermistors: Typically made from silicon, these devices have a relatively stable positive temperature coefficient. Their resistance increases approximately linearly with temperature, making them suitable for temperature measurement applications. Simply put, an NTC thermistor behaves like a component that offers less resistance as it gets hotter. A linear PTC thermistor works in the opposite way: its resistance increases with temperature, generally in a more uniform and predictable manner. 2. Voltage Divider Circuit (Constant-Voltage Excitation) Figure 2. Thermistor in a voltage divider configuration This is one of the simplest and most cost-effective thermistor measurement methods. A thermistor is connected in series with a fixed reference resistor and supplied by a stable voltage source, such as VCC. By measuring the voltage across one of the resistors, the temperature information can be obtained. Working Principle: When the temperature changes, the thermistor's resistance changes accordingly. According to the voltage divider principle, the output voltage, V_TEMP, also changes. By measuring this voltage, the thermistor resistance can be calculated, and the corresponding temperature can then be determined. Considerations: Variations in the supply voltage VCC can affect V_TEMP and introduce measurement errors. To reduce this effect, a ratiometric measurement method can be used. For example, the same voltage source can serve as both the excitation voltage for the divider and the ADC reference voltage. This helps cancel out the effects of supply voltage fluctuations. Constant-Current Excitation Circuit Figure 3. Working Principle: According to Ohm's law, V = I × R. Since the current flowing through the thermistor remains constant, the voltage across it, V_TEMP, is proportional to its resistance: V TEMP = I BIAS × R THERMISTOR When the temperature changes and the thermistor resistance varies, the output voltage changes accordingly. Advantages: Within the operating range of the current source, the output voltage is linearly proportional to the thermistor resistance. This makes resistance measurement and signal processing more straightforward, especially in applications requiring relatively high measurement accuracy. Considerations: The accuracy, temperature drift, and output voltage range of the current source all affect measurement results. In addition, excessive excitation current can cause thermistor self-heating. Therefore, the bias current must be selected carefully. The Next Step: Signal Processing The resulting analog voltage signal, V TEMP , is typically sent to an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) input on a microcontroller (MCU) for digital processing. Alternatively, it can be sent to a voltage comparator and compared with a preset threshold voltage to implement a basic overtemperature alarm. Figure 4. Its relatively linear characteristics can simplify temperature conversion, but the actual measurement accuracy, operating range, and calibration requirements must still be evaluated based on the specific device specifications. In practical designs, thermistor measurement performance depends not only on the sensor itself but also on the excitation circuit, ADC configuration, sensor placement, and thermistor PCB layout. By considering component selection, circuit design, and PCB layout together, designers can develop more accurate and reliable temperature monitoring systems. Verify Now Blog > PCB Ground Plane Design: Routing Across Plane Splits and Signal Return Paths PCB Ground Plane Design: Routing Across Plane Splits and Signal Return Paths by: Mila Nov 19,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb ground plane pcb ground plane design decoupling capacitor layout signal return path A well-designed PCB ground plane is essential for maintaining signal integrity, controlling electromagnetic interference (EMI), and providing low-impedance return paths. However, issues such as split reference planes, improper signal routing, and poor decoupling capacitor placement can interrupt return-current paths and affect circuit performance. This article discusses several practical PCB ground plane design considerations, including routing across plane splits, maintaining continuous return paths, optimizing decoupling capacitor pcb layout , and managing copper pours. 1. Do Differential Pairs Need a Reference Plane? For differential signals, the electromagnetic coupling between the two signal traces is fundamental to their operation. The differential-mode current primarily forms a loop between the two traces. Therefore, tight coupling between the differential pair helps reduce the loop area and minimize external interference. However, does this mean that differential pairs do not need a reference plane? The answer is no. Due to limitations in component packaging, PCB manufacturing processes, and actual routing conditions, it is difficult to achieve perfect symmetry between the two traces. Factors such as connectors, vias, pads, and routing discontinuities can also introduce common-mode components into differential signals. These common-mode currents require the reference plane and other associated structures to provide a return path. Therefore, differential pairs need not only good coupling between the two traces but also appropriate electromagnetic coupling with the nearby reference plane. During PCB layout, use a continuous and solid reference plane whenever possible, and avoid routing differential signals across plane splits. 2. How to Route Signals Across Plane Splits When a signal trace crosses different reference plane regions, the return current may lose its continuous path. This can increase the current loop area and parasitic inductance, potentially causing signal integrity and EMI problems. Therefore, avoid routing signals across reference plane splits whenever possible. If this cannot be avoided due to circuit constraints, the appropriate solution depends on the type of plane being crossed. Routing Across Ground Plane Splits For two physically separated regions belonging to the same GND net, prioritize maintaining a continuous return path by establishing a proper connection between the ground areas. If the two ground planes belong to different ground nets, such as analog ground and digital ground, their connection should be determined according to the system grounding architecture. Components such as resistors or ferrite beads may be used to connect the two ground nets at designated locations. However, simply adding a resistor or ferrite bead does not solve every ground plane splitting issue. （Routing across a ground plane split） Routing Across Power Plane Splits When a signal crosses two different power reference regions, an appropriate high-frequency bypass capacitor can be placed between the two power planes to provide a return path for the current. The capacitor should be placed as close as possible to the signal crossing point, with short, low-inductance connections to the two reference regions. The capacitor's equivalent series inductance (ESL), as well as the parasitic inductance introduced by vias and connecting traces, must also be considered. However, this does not mean that signals can freely cross power plane splits. For high-speed signals, routing on a layer with a continuous reference plane remains the more reliable approach. (Using a capacitor to provide a return path across a power plane split) Using Jumpers to Cross Routing Paths When signal traces cross each other and the routing cannot be resolved by adjusting the routing layers or trace paths, a jumper can be used to bridge one trace over another and prevent a direct electrical connection. (jumper routing example) Adding Ground Stitching Vias When Changing Signal Layers When a signal changes routing layers through a via, it is also important to consider whether its reference plane changes. For example, when a signal transitions from the top layer to another signal layer, the two layers may reference different GND planes. In this case, the return current must also transition from the original reference plane to the new one. If there is no low-impedance connection between the two reference planes, the return current may be forced to take a longer path, increasing the current loop inductance. Therefore, ground stitching vias can be placed near the signal transition via to provide a more direct return path for the current. (Adding GND vias near a signal layer transition) 3. PCB Decoupling Capacitor Layout Guidelines The effectiveness of a decoupling capacitor depends not only on its capacitance but also on its placement, connection method, and power return path on the PCB. If the capacitor is placed too far from the IC power pin, or if its connecting traces and vias are too long, additional parasitic inductance will be introduced, reducing its high-frequency decoupling performance. Therefore, during PCB layout, the current loop between the decoupling capacitor and the IC should be kept as short as possible. Keep Decoupling Capacitors Close to IC Power Pins Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as possible to the IC power pins, especially for high-speed digital ICs and devices with rapidly changing transient current demands. During placement, minimize the connection length between the power pin and the capacitor, while also shortening the return path from the capacitor's GND terminal to the ground plane. (Decoupling capacitor placement around an IC) Optimize the Power and Ground Return Paths Proper decoupling capacitor placement involves more than positioning the capacitor close to the IC. The power and GND connections must also be carefully routed. For power circuits, minimize the high-frequency switching current loop area and avoid interference between high-current return paths and sensitive signal return paths. (Correct decoupling capacitor placement and routing) For the GND connections in power loops, plan the return paths according to the circuit topology. Avoid sharing long, narrow traces between high-current return paths and sensitive signal grounds. However, this does not mean that power ground and signal ground must always be physically separated. In designs with a solid GND plane, the more important consideration is controlling the current flow to prevent large common-impedance voltage drops in sensitive signal areas. (power loop GND and signal ground) (Examples of different GND return path layouts) Minimize the IPM Power Supply Return Loop For power devices such as IPMs (Intelligent Power Modules), the design of the main power supply return path is particularly important. The main power loop area should be minimized, and the GND return path should connect directly back to the main bulk capacitor at the power supply input, avoiding unnecessary detours. This helps reduce parasitic inductance, voltage spikes during switching, and electromagnetic interference. (IPM main power supply return path) Connect Digital Ground Copper to the Main Ground Plane In digital signal areas, GND copper can be poured on the surface layer and connected to the main GND plane through multiple GND stitching vias. These vias help reduce the connection impedance between different GND regions and provide additional paths for high-frequency return currents. However, the number and spacing of vias should be determined according to signal frequency, routing density, and the actual return path requirements. More vias do not necessarily mean better performance. (Connecting digital ground copper to the main GND plane using a row of GND vias) 4. Why Should Decoupling Capacitors Have Separate Ground Vias? Different decoupling capacitors are typically used to suppress power supply noise across different frequency ranges. If multiple capacitors share the same GND via or a long common return path, the shared path inductance may cause them to interfere with one another. For example, when one capacitor supplies current to an IC during a transient event, the changing current generates a voltage across the parasitic inductance of the shared via. This voltage variation may couple into the return path of another capacitor, reducing its decoupling effectiveness. Therefore, for high-frequency decoupling capacitors, it is recommended to provide independent, short, and low-inductance GND connections whenever practical. Avoid sharing connection paths with significant parasitic inductance. It is important to note that sharing a via does not always cause serious problems. The actual impact depends on the current, operating frequency, connection structure, and parasitic parameters of the shared path. (Multiple decoupling capacitors sharing a GND via) 5. How to Handle Connector and Interface Routing Connector and interface routing must also account for signal interference and the continuity of return paths. For interfaces carrying high-speed signals, maintain a continuous reference plane beneath the signals whenever possible. For interfaces containing differential pairs, pay particular attention to differential impedance control, trace spacing, and length matching. For connectors with a large number of pins, GND pins should be arranged appropriately to provide nearby return paths for signals and reduce crosstalk between them. 6. For example, a four-layer PCB with a solid inner GND plane does not necessarily need GND copper poured on every other layer. When properly implemented, it can improve the electrical and thermal performance of a PCB while also benefiting the manufacturing process. The main benefits include: Improved EMI Shielding: Continuous and properly grounded surface copper can provide additional shielding for inner-layer signals, helping reduce certain types of external interference. Better Heat Dissipation: Copper pours can expand the area available for heat conduction and distribution. However, the actual thermal performance also depends on copper thickness, copper area, and thermal connection methods. Reduced Copper Etchant Consumption: Under certain conditions, properly designed copper pours can reduce the amount of copper that needs to be removed during the PCB etching process. Improved Copper Balance: Distributing copper more evenly can improve copper balance across the PCB and reduce the risk of warpage caused by uneven copper distribution during manufacturing. Potential Problems with Fragmented Ground Copper More surface copper does not necessarily mean better PCB performance. The surface layer usually contains numerous components, pads, and signal traces, which can divide GND copper into multiple disconnected regions. If these regions are not properly connected to the main GND plane through sufficient vias, they may become floating copper areas or regions with high-impedance connections. In particular, long, narrow, and isolated copper sections may introduce unwanted parasitic coupling and, under certain conditions, behave like antennas, potentially causing EMI problems. (Fragmented copper areas caused by surface routing) Remove Unnecessary Ground Copper Areas Unnecessary fragmented copper areas that cannot be properly grounded or provide no practical benefit to signal return paths can be removed using the copper removal features in PCB design software. For example, in a four-layer PCB that already has a solid inner GND plane, priority should be given to maintaining the integrity of the main GND plane. Unnecessary fragmented GND copper on other layers can be removed. However, this does not mean that all surface GND copper should be removed. If the surface copper remains continuous and is properly connected to the main ground plane through strategically placed GND vias, it can still provide additional shielding, heat dissipation, and high-frequency return paths. PCB ground plane design involves more than simply adding copper to unused areas of a board. Maintaining continuous reference planes, providing proper return paths, and minimizing parasitic inductance are all important for reliable signal transmission and power distribution. By considering these factors during PCB layout , designers can reduce signal integrity issues, improve EMI performance, and achieve more reliable circuit operation.
