events.after: Resources / Materials / Silica Gel: Purpose, Origin, How Is It Made, Types, and Uses Silica Gel: Purpose, Origin, How Is It Made, Types, and Uses Written by Dean McClements 15 min read Published January 3, 2024 Updated November 10, 2026 Silica gel is applied as a desiccant and used to control moisture and humidity levels in a spectrum of applications. Its primary function is to adsorb and retain airborne or contact-surface moisture. This serves to prevent the growth/progress of mold/mildew, corrosion, and other moisture-related damage issues in products. There are several forms of silica gel, generally considered as indicating and non-indicating varieties. Indicating silica gel undergoes color changes, often from blue to pink, as the indicator chemical additive absorbs the moisture. Non-indicating silica gel doesn't change color but adsorbs moisture equally effectively. Silica gel is manufactured in a range of particle sizes and shapes for specific applications. This article will discuss what silica gel is, how it is made, its purpose, origin, types, and uses. What Is a Silica Gel? Silica gel is a versatile and efficacious desiccant used to absorb and hold moisture from its local environment. It is a solid particulate material, but its name derives from the gelation process used to manufacture it. It consists of tiny, nano-porous beads or crystals of silicon dioxide. The key characteristic of silica gel is its extreme ability to adsorb water vapor and virtually any aqueous substance. Its extraordinarily fine porosity results in a massive functional surface area, allowing it to trap and hold moisture molecules on its extensive surface. This essentially isolates the water from surrounding surfaces, preventing damage or degradation in products and materials thus protected. Its moisture-adsorbing capabilities make it a valuable tool for controlling humidity and protecting against the chemical and biological effects of moisture in most product and industrial contexts. What Is the Other Term for Silica Gel? An alternative name for silica gel is silicic acid gel , which is a more accurate description of the chemistry. Silica gel is the commercial nomenclature, whereas silicic acid gel is more precise and used in scientific or technical contexts. Is Silica Gel and Silica Desiccant the Same? Yes, silica gel and silica desiccant are considered in most contexts to be the same thing. Desiccant is a generalized term covering any substance or material used to absorb and remove moisture from its surroundings, and silica gel is the most commonly used but not the only desiccant chemical. What Does Silica Gel Look Like? Silica gel typically appears as small, translucent, or semi-translucent beads or crystals, in sizes ranging from particles as small as grains of sand up to small (2 mm) beads. It is naturally white or colorless but manufactured in various colors for specific applications. Some silica gel products contain indicator beads that alter in color as they become saturated, flagging the need for regeneration or replacement. What Does Silica Gel Do? Silica gel products primarily serve as desiccants. They absorb and retain moisture from their surroundings. The material is derived from its mineral sources in various forms and serves a purpose by moderating atmospheric and surface moisture. This helps to protect products, environments, and materials from the degradation that results from wet oxidation and biological growth. Why Is Silica Gel Important in Manufacturing? Silica gel is important in manufacturing for various related reasons as listed below: Manufacturing processes often require precise control over or minimization of humidity levels. Silica gel helps maintain the target level, preventing issues such as powder clumping, deterioration of raw materials, and damage to finished products. Used to preserve the quality of various materials, including chemicals, pharmaceuticals, and food products by preventing moisture-induced degradation from aqueous chemical or biological processes. Manufacturing equipment can be highly sensitive to moisture which results in corrosion. Silica gel helps protect such sensitive assets by desiccating the environment. In electronics manufacturing, moisture control is critical to prevent defects and ensure product reliability, both at a component and product level. Employed in the packaging of manufactured goods to control humidity risks in shipping and storage, maintaining optimal conditions. In pharmaceuticals and semiconductor manufacturing, stringent environmental controls can be imperative. Silica gel helps maintain controlled humidity levels in cleanrooms and manufacturing environments. What Is the Origin of Silica Gel? Silica gel has been known since the mid-17th Century, but its first actual application was as an aqueous airborne toxin removal mechanism in gas masks (in which role it is still employed). A manufacturing process was first patented by Walter Patrick of Johns Hopkins University in 1919. The material found high-value use during the Second World War, employed as a catalyst for the production of gasoline with extreme octane levels and in the making of butadiene, the monomer used in the manufacture of synthetic rubbers. What Is Silica Gel Made Of? Silica gel is produced by chemically processing sodium metasilicate (Na2SiO3), sodium orthosilicate (Na4SiO4), and sodium pyrosilicate (Na6Si2O7) to form high-purity silicon dioxide (SiO2). The sodium silicates are a naturally occurring mineral group, commonly co-deposited with quartz, sand, and other minerals. The refined product is manufactured through an acidic gelation process followed by drying. Silica gel is silicic acid, alternatively silicon dioxide (SiO2). What Are the Properties of Silica Gel? The properties of silica gel are listed in Table 1 below: Table 1: Properties of Silica Gel Is It Possible To Make a DIY Silica Gel? No. Creating DIY silica gel is challenging due to the precise chemical processes involved in its production. Attempting to replicate the manufacturing process at home is complex, demanding specialized equipment and chemicals and precise process control. What Are Silica Gel Packets Made Of? Silica gel packets are typically made of a material called Tyvek® or other lower-cost, non-woven polypropylene or polyethylene fabrics. These materials are open to air and moisture transfer but have very fine pore size which prevents powder escape. The fabric is unaffected by moisture but may limit the regeneration temperature of the finished packet. The fabric packets are usually heat-sealed or ultrasonically sealed to contain the silica gel inside the fabric pouch. What Are the Different Types of Silica Gel? The different types of silica gel are listed and discussed below: 1. Type A Silica Gel Type A silica gel is generally available as very clear pellets that are nano-porous with typically 40 Å (Angstrom) pores. Applied in product packaging, this type of silica gel protects moisture-sensitive items from humidity-related damage. It is also employed in industrial settings for moisture control in manufacturing processes and for preserving the quality of various materials and products. This material is important in chromatography and catalytic-support roles, ensuring extreme exposure of a target chemical/reaction to the catalyst by applying it on the extensive surface area that the silica gel’s nano-porosity provides. Silica gel's very high chemical stability prevents stray reactions in catalytic applications, as the gel is essentially inert in most contexts. This class of material is widely used in the gas separation columns of gas chromatographs. 2. Type B Silica Gel Type B silica gel is translucent white and has nano-porosity in the range of 4.5–7.0 nm, which alters the transparency. Also applied as a desiccant, this material is lower cost and used whenever the pore size is appropriate or as a constituent in scent reduction applications such as cat litter, in which cost is a larger concern. In higher purity forms, it also serves in gas chromatography applications and as a catalyst exposure/support mechanism. 3. Type C Silica Gel Type C silica gels have large pore sizes and a surface that is populated by silicon-hydride (Si-H) groups as opposed to silanols (Si-OH). They’re widely used as desiccants across most sectors and as catalyst carriers for the manufacture of butadiene synthetic rubber, melamine polymer (cyanamide), and acrylic nitrite. These materials are frequently employed in petrochemical refining, adsorption of organics in gas and liquid states, and aqueous phase chromatography applications like high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). 4. Stabilizing Silica Gel Stabilizing silica gel is specific to the stabilization and preservation of high volatility and contamination-sensitive compounds in the pharmaceutical and organic chemistry sectors. It presents a chemically modified surface that restrains interactions between the silica gel and the process materials, reducing reactive contaminant formation. Stabilizing silica gel plays a critical role in maintaining the quality and serviceability of high-sensitivity materials, as a tool for various industries. 5. Silica Alumina Gel Silica alumina gel is a composite material that combines silica gel and alumina. It is used as a catalyst carrier agent or adsorbent in various chemical and industrial processes. This material is often employed in applications that require specific catalytic or molecular-sieve adsorption properties, such as in the petroleum and petrochemical industries for refining and chemical manufacturing by catalytic cracking, hydrocracking, and adsorption of impurities. Silica alumina gel’s composition can vary, as the relative proportions of silica and alumina are adjusted to achieve specific performance criteria, such as: acidity, surface area, and pore-size distribution. This versatility makes silica-alumina gel valuable for a range of applications. What Are the Uses of Silica Gel? Silica gel has a wide range of uses due to its excellent moisture-absorbing properties and safety. Some of its key applications include: Silica gel packets are commonly placed in product packaging to protect items sensitive to moisture, such as: electronics, pharmaceuticals, and food products. Assist in the prevention of moisture damage and deterioration of important documents, photographs, and high-value items, and they are widely used in museums for this purpose. Are extensively used in chemical processing and catalyst support roles, across the oil & gas, polymers, and organic chemistry industries. As desiccants, they are used to protect sensitive electronic components and circuitry from humidity-related issues, ensuring product reliability. Moisture-induced excess oxidation of component solder points makes them immediately unusable in automated reflow and wave soldering applications, as the more aggressive fluxes used to remove such heavier oxidation are impractical in other regards. Are employed to prevent fogging on camera lenses, eyeglasses, sealed double-glazing modules, and optical equipment in storage or internal to sealed assemblies. When saturated and exposed to elevated temperatures, evaporation and temporary condensation/fogging are real risks in sealed products. How To Properly Use Silica Gel? To apply silica gel effectively, the following tips should be observed: Use an appropriate quantity of silica gel for the size of the container or area/volume you want to protect. Ensure the grade selected is appropriate for the task. More complex tasks such as chemical catalysis and molecular sieve applications require very specific properties. Make sure the container or space is properly sealed to prevent moisture from entering. Rapid saturation in open environments with elevated humidity negates all use in the materials. Monitor the silica gel regularly for color changes (for indicating types) and replace or regenerate it as needed. To regenerate, heat the silica gel in an oven at the recommended temperature for a specific time (as per the manufacturer's instructions). Avoid contact with eyes and the respiratory tract and ingestion. Store silica gel packets out of reach of children and pets. Can Silica Gel be Used on Galvanized Steel? Yes, silica gel can be used on galvanized steel to protect it from moisture-related issues, such as corrosion. Placing silica gel packets in sealed storage containers helps maintain a dry environment. What Is the Recommended Amount of Silica Gel? Recommendations as to the quantity of silica gel in desiccant applications depend on several factors, including: the size of the enclosed space, the humidity levels, and the specific moisture control requirements. A general guideline is to use about 28–85 grams per cubic meter of an enclosed space. Using too little silica gel may not provide sufficient protection, while using too much may lead to over-drying and unnecessary regeneration. In many cases, manufacturers will offer guidelines that can provide support in deciding quantity. What Happens if Silica Gel Gets Wet? When silica gel gets wet, it becomes saturated with moisture. As it wets, its moisture-absorbing capacity degrades progressively until it can no longer effectively adsorb. The gel may turn translucent or change color if it's an indicating type. If left wet for an extended period, it can develop mold and may become less effective or unusable as regeneration can leave organic detritus that reduces its porosity. What Are the Precautions for Using Silica Gel? When using silica gel, it's essential to take certain precautions to ensure people and environmental safety and the effectiveness of the product. These are: Silica gel is not meant for consumption, so keep it away from children and pets. The dust residue of the material can become airborne and will severely irritate the eyes and mucus membranes, so use caution (good quality PPE is required for prolonged contact or extensive exposure). Handle silica gel and pack with clean, dry hands to maintain its effectiveness. When not in use, store the packets in airtight containers to prevent premature moisture absorption. If regenerating silica gel by heating, do so in a well-ventilated area to avoid inhaling fumes of adsorbed residues that will volatilize, potentially in concentrated amounts. Dispose of silica gel by local regulations. Some types can be discarded with regular waste, while others may need special handling. What Happens if Someone Eats Silica Gel? Silica gel is considered to be non-toxic, but it is not meant for consumption. Eating it is not advisable, but if a small amount is ingested, it is unlikely to cause significant harm. It can result in digestive discomfort — irritation or mild gastrointestinal symptoms such as upset stomach or diarrhea. Although the material is graded as not highly toxic, it's wise to act with caution and seek medical advice, in the event of consumption. Can Silica Gel Be Used To Store Food Safely? No. Silica gel is not suited for direct contact with food, despite being considered non-toxic. Instead, it is securely packaged, generally in a non-woven fabric sleeve, and used to control moisture and humidity within the storage packaging of food items, to reduce the incidence/rate of moisture-related damage. Food-grade silica gel is specifically designed for this purpose, meeting strict safety standards for contact with food (when contained appropriately). How Much Does Silica Gel Cost? The retail/wholesale price of silica gel varies very widely, depending on several factors, including: the type, purity, quantity, and source. Small silica gel pockets for packaging and protecting consumer products can cost as little as a few cents each. When purchased in larger quantities, the cost per unit of silica gel decreases. Bulk quantities may range from a few dollars per pound or kilogram. Indicating silica gel is often slightly more expensive than non-indicating silica gel, due to the increased complexity of manufacture. Some specialized types of silica gel, such as stabilizing silica gel used in pharmaceuticals or chromatography column materials can be considerably more expensive due to their specific properties and applications. These can cost several hundred dollars per lb/kg. What Are the Benefits of Silica Gel? Silica gel offers various benefits that depend heavily on the nature of the application, such as: Its most exploited benefit is its exceptional moisture-absorbing ability. Serves to extend the shelf life and quality of products, from electronics to documents and collectibles. Indicating silica gel provides a visual signal when it's saturated, indicating the need for replacement or regeneration. These materials are safe and non-toxic, making them suitable for pharmaceutical and food-related applications. Most types of silica gel can be regenerated and reused multiple times by heating to dry the material. They are generally environmentally neutral materials and can be disposed of according to local regulations without pollution risk, depending on the nature of the application and contaminants. What Are the Risks of Silica Gel? While silica gel is generally safe for its intended purposes, there are a few risks associated with it such as: Ingestion. Eye, mucus membrane, and skin irritation. Respiratory tract irritation. Vapor release of captured materials during regeneration. Is Silica Gel Reusable? Yes. However, if highly saturated with volatiles, as may be the case from a polymer catalyst or hydrocarbon purification process, the resultant evaporites may pose a flammability risk. events.before: Resources / Materials / Stainless Steel vs. Tungsten: What Are the Key Differences? Stainless Steel vs. Tungsten: What Are the Key Differences? Written by Dean McClements Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 16 min read Published January 31, 2024 Updated November 20, 2026 Stainless steel and tungsten are distinct materials with differences in composition, properties, and applications. Stainless steel is an alloy made primarily of iron and chromium, with nickel and other elements added in some grades, and its properties vary depending on the grade. Tungsten is a chemical element with the symbol "W" on the periodic table. It is a transition metal with an exceptionally high melting point and density. Stainless steel is extremely widely used across all industries, including construction, automotive, kitchenware, medical equipment, consumer goods, and outdoor furniture, due to its corrosion resistance and versatility. Tungsten, on the other hand, is used extensively in armor-piercing projectiles, penetrators, and counterweights because of its density and hardness. This article will discuss the key differences between stainless steel and tungsten in terms of composition, types, and applications. What Is Stainless Steel? Stainless steel is a family of alloys, composed of iron, chromium, nickel, and varying amounts of elements like molybdenum, manganese, and silicon. Its remarkable corrosion resistance stems from the formation of a passive chromium oxide layer on its surface when exposed to oxygen. This protective layer prevents rust and deterioration, even in humid or chemically aggressive environments. Stainless steel offers great durability at a relatively low cost, putting this family of alloys at the heart of products in construction, automotive, aerospace, consumer goods, healthcare, industrial processing, and many other sectors. With various grades and types available, stainless steel can be tuned to meet specific requirements, optimizing its value in various applications and more demanding conditions, by careful selection of alloying constituents and heat treatment. To learn more, see our full guide on the Properties of Stainless Steel . What Is Another Name for Stainless Steel? Stainless steel is sometimes referred to as corrosion-resistant steel. It is also called inox, from the French inoxydable, meaning non-oxidizable. What Is Stainless Steel Made Of? Stainless steel’s constituent alloying elements include iron (Fe), chromium (Cr), nickel (Ni), molybdenum (Mo), manganese (Mn), and silicon (Si), with cobalt (Co) only rarely used in specialized grades. The combination and ratios of these alloying agents, along with the manufacturing processes, determine the resulting grade and properties of stainless steel. The divergent grades of stainless steel exhibit alternate crystalline structures that significantly affect the material properties, the level of corrosion resistance, strength, ductility, temperature resistance, and other characteristics. This results in a large family of materials that offer characteristics suitable for a wide range of industrial and commercial applications. How Is Stainless Steel Made? Stainless steels are produced by melting iron with carefully selected alloying elements, primarily chromium, in a controlled furnace process to achieve the desired composition. It begins with a careful selection of raw materials, including iron, scrap steel of known constituents, and selected additions from chromium, nickel, molybdenum, and others. The selection of metals defines the outcome of stainless steel grade and its properties. The selected raw materials are melted in an electric arc or induction furnace at extremely high temperatures. Strict control over temperature and composition is required to achieve precise alloying ratios. Alloying elements are introduced into the molten iron/scrap steel to attain the precise composition needed for the desired grade. These alloying elements are often added in the form of pre-prepared alloy or pure metal ingots. Deoxidizing and desulfurizing agents may be used during the melting process to remove impurities like oxygen and sulfur. Common deoxidizers include silicon, aluminum, and manganese. Sulfur is typically controlled with additives like calcium or rare-earth elements. Samples are taken from the melt for spectroscopic analysis to ensure that the alloying elements are within the specified range. This QC measure guarantees that the final stainless steel product meets industry standards and customer requirements. Once properly alloyed and tested, the molten steel is cast into semi-finished forms such as slabs, billets, or ingots. This can be continuous or batch casting, depending on the scale of production. What Are the Different Types of Stainless Steel? Stainless steel can be classified into several main classes or types based on its microstructure and alloy composition, with fine degrees of differentiation in subcategories of alloys with highly tuned properties. Below are the different types of stainless steel : Austenitic Stainless Steel : These steels are the most common and widely used type of stainless steel. They have a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure and are generally non-magnetic, although they can become slightly magnetic when cold-worked. Renowned for its excellent corrosion resistance, high ductility, and good formability, the common grades include 304 (18-8 stainless), 316 (sometimes called marine-grade), and 321. Ferritic Stainless Steel : They are formed from a body-centered cubic (BCC) crystalline structure. They are magnetic and offer good corrosion resistance, especially in environments with low chloride content. Common grades include 430 and 409. Martensitic Stainless Steel : They transform from austenite to martensite on quenching, giving them a body-centered tetragonal (BCT) crystal structure at room temperature. Duplex Stainless Steel : Duplex stainless steels combine the properties of both austenitic and ferritic stainless steels. They have a mixed microstructure of austenite and ferrite, which provides excellent corrosion resistance and high strength. Common grades include 2205 and 2507 (Super Duplex). Illustration of duplex steel. Precipitation-Hardening Stainless Steel : Precipitation-hardening stainless steels can be heat-treated to achieve elevated levels of strength and hardness. They can be martensitic or austenitic. They are used in applications in which both corrosion resistance and good mechanical properties are critical. Grades include 17-4 PH (martensitic), 15-5 PH (martensitic), 17-7 PH (semi-austenitic), PH 15-7 Mo (semi-austenitic), and JBK-75 (austenitic). Some sources also list FV520, though it is less common. Specialty Stainless Steels : Various specialty grades have been developed for specific applications. Examples include high-temperature grades such as 310 or 446 stainless, low-carbon grades like 304L, and other corrosion-resistant alloys such as Inconel® (though Inconel is not stainless steel but a separate nickel-based superalloy family). Each class of stainless steel has its own optimized properties. Grade selection is crucial to ensuring the resultant product performance and longevity in real-world use environments. What Are the Advantages of Stainless Steel? Stainless steels offer numerous advantages, varied by grade and allowing selection for particular properties that are advantageous for each application: Has exceptional corrosion resistance, making it ideal for harsh environments. Each grade has particular environmental resilience and susceptibilities that can be closely identified. Robust and generally tolerant of wear, impact, and moderately high temperatures, although extreme abrasion or very high temperatures require specialized grades. Provides smooth, non-porous, and durable surfaces that are easy to clean, making stainless steel suitable for food, medical, and pharmaceutical applications. Provide various degrees of mechanical properties, including good tensile strength, though most grades are not as hard as tool steels unless specially treated (e.g., martensitic or precipitation-hardening grades). Adaptable to various industries, from construction and automotive to healthcare and aerospace. Can deliver a sleek appearance and reflective surfaces, making them popular in architectural and decorative applications. Highly recyclable and resistant to process degradation and material loss, promoting sustainability. What Are the Disadvantages of Stainless Steel? While stainless steel offers many advantages across many applications, it also has particular and more generalized disadvantages, such as: It can be more expensive than other materials due to its complex alloy composition and increased difficulty in manufacturing processes. Some grades, such as ferritic and martensitic stainless steels, can become embrittled at low temperatures, while austenitic stainless steels generally retain toughness even in cryogenic conditions. It can be challenging to machine and may require specialized tools and processes. This is particularly true of the austenitic grades, which can demonstrate severe work hardening during cutting processes. Its relatively high density compared to aluminum or titanium makes stainless steel less suitable for weight-sensitive applications. Has lower thermal conductivity compared to other metals like aluminum or copper. Despite this, these materials are often used in heat-exchange applications in which the need for chemical resilience outweighs the thermal limitations. Ferritic and martensitic stainless steels are magnetic, while austenitic grades are generally non-magnetic (though they can become slightly magnetic after cold working), which can affect their suitability for applications such as MRI machines and other sensitive instruments. It can show fingerprints or water spots in a very pronounced way, although they can be easily cleaned. The production of stainless steel can have a significant environmental footprint due to energy-intensive processes and environmentally degrading mining and refining processes. In particular, chromium mining and refining can produce toxic byproducts such as hexavalent chromium, which requires strict environmental controls. Is Stainless Steel Better Than Tungsten? It depends on the specific application. Stainless steel excels in corrosion resistance and versatility, but does not possess tungsten's extreme hardness and high-temperature resilience. Tungsten is ideal for certain high-wear and very high-temperature applications due to its hardness and high melting point, but it is also denser and significantly more expensive than stainless steel. What Is Tungsten? Tungsten is a chemical element (symbol W, atomic number 74) from the transition metals group. It is extremely dense and has the highest melting point of all metals (about 3420 °C). These properties make tungsten valuable in applications such as electrical wires and filaments, high-temperature jet and rocket parts, and as an alloying element in steel to improve hardness and durability. Tungsten is also used to create tungsten carbide, an extremely hard compound widely used in cutting tools, wear-resistant parts, and abrasives. What Is Another Name for Tungsten? Tungsten is known as “wolfram,” originating from German miners who observed tungsten minerals interfering with tin smelting, “devouring” the tin like a wolf. This gave rise to the symbol W on the periodic table. The name “tungsten” is derived from the Swedish words “tung sten,” meaning “heavy stone,” a reference to its density. What Is Tungsten Made Of? Tungsten is a chemical element and consists of an indivisible atomic structure. Tungsten's high atomic number informs of a heavy nucleus that gives it its unique properties, such as its exceptionally high melting point, hardness, and density. How Is Tungsten Made? Tungsten is produced from ores such as wolframite and scheelite through mining, ore concentration, chemical processing, and metallurgical purification. Chemical processing transforms the ore into ammonium paratungstate (APT) or tungstic acid. A reduction process using hydrogen converts APT into tungsten metal powder, typically at high temperatures. Further purification removes impurities, and consolidation methods/smelting create solid forms. These are then machined and shaped into desired products. What Are the Different Types of Tungsten? Tungsten-containing materials encompass a wide range of products and compounds: Tungsten-Bearing Alloys : Tungsten is often alloyed with other metals like nickel, copper, or iron to create high-density materials with enhanced properties. Common examples include tungsten-copper (for hard-wearing, arc-resistant electrical contacts) and tungsten-nickel-iron alloys (for radiation shielding). Tungsten Carbide : Tungsten carbide is a hard and wear-resistant compound formed by combining tungsten and carbon, typically produced by sintering tungsten carbide powder with a metal binder such as cobalt. It's used extensively in cutting tools, drills, saw blades, and machining inserts. Tungsten Filaments : Tungsten is used in the manufacturing of incandescent lightbulbs and electron-microscope filaments due to its high melting point and electrical conductivity. Tungsten Compounds : Tungsten is found in various chemical compounds, such as tungstic acid (H2WO4) and ammonium paratungstate (APT), precursors in the refining of tungsten metal. Tungsten-Based Superalloys : Tungsten is used as a strengthening element in some nickel- and cobalt-based superalloys, where it improves high-temperature strength and creep resistance for aerospace and power-generation applications such as turbine blades and combustion components. Tungsten Target Materials : In the semiconductor industry, tungsten is used as a target material for sputtering to deposit thin films on semiconductor wafers. Its stability and high-temperature performance leave it unaffected by the sputtering process. Tungsten Heavy Alloys : Typically, tungsten-nickel-iron or tungsten-nickel-copper are used where high density, strength, and radiation shielding are required. Tungsten Wire and Rods : These are used in electrical and heating applications, including thermocouples and heating elements. What Are the Advantages of Tungsten? Tungsten offers some pronounced and unique advantages: Has one of the highest melting points of any element, making it ideal for extreme-temperature applications in aerospace and metallurgy. It is extremely hard, providing excellent wear resistance valued in cutting tools, drills, and abrasives. Its density is close to that of gold (at a considerably lower cost), making it applicable for balancing, radiation shielding, and military-projectile applications. Tungsten is moderately resistant to corrosion in many environments, but it oxidizes at relatively low temperatures in air and is less corrosion-resistant than stainless steels or noble metals. Tungsten has moderate electrical conductivity, lower than copper or silver, but sufficient for applications such as lamp filaments, X-ray tubes, and electrical contacts. What Are the Disadvantages of Tungsten? While tungsten has many advantages, it also has some significant disadvantages that limit its applicability: It is relatively expensive due to its scarcity and challenging extraction/refining process. Tungsten exhibits a high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature, typically between 200 °C and 400 °C, which limits the use of pure tungsten at lower temperatures. Its high density makes tungsten heavier than many other materials, which is a burden whenever it is a necessary material in weight-sensitive applications. It is difficult to machine, requiring specialized tools and techniques that tungsten CNC machining services are set up to handle. Its compounds can be toxic, particularly when inhaled as dust or fumes during processing. Tungsten mining and processing have a significant environmental footprint due to energy-intensive and toxic intermediate processes. Certain tungsten alloys containing ferromagnetic elements such as iron or cobalt can be magnetic, which may affect their suitability for specific applications. Is Tungsten Better Than Stainless Steel? It depends on the specifics of the application. Tungsten excels in extreme hardness, very high melting point, and density. Stainless steel offers a balance of good strength, corrosion resistance, relatively lower cost compared to tungsten, and broad versatility across industries. How To Choose Between Stainless Steel and Tungsten? The selection between tungsten and stainless steel depends on the specific requirements of the application. Understand the key factors, such as service temperature, corrosion challenges, strength, and cost issues that are critical for your application. Choose tungsten if you need extreme hardness, a very high melting point, or maximum density. Choose stainless steel if corrosion resistance, versatility, and cost-effectiveness are priorities. Assess the budget available for materials, as tungsten is far more expensive than stainless steel and is generally used only when its unique properties are essential. Based on your project requirements, evaluate the ease of machining and fabricating of each material. As a rule, higher production volumes and complex machining operations favor stainless steel since tungsten is very difficult and costly to machine. How To Identify Stainless Steel and Tungsten? Various methods can be used to identify stainless steel and tungsten. Stainless steels are generally non-magnetic or less markedly magnetic than mild or carbon steels. If a magnet doesn't attract, it's likely stainless steel. They typically have a shiny, reflective surface, often with a brushed or polished finish. Check for manufacturer markings or labels on the material to identify the grade. Stainless steel is generally highly corrosion-resistant and won't rust easily when exposed to moisture in natural environments. Tungsten, on the other hand, remains stable in ambient air at room temperature but oxidizes at elevated temperatures (above about 400 °C), forming tungsten oxides. Tungsten is exceptionally dense and heavy; it will feel much heavier than materials of similar size. It has a distinct metallic gray color with a high luster. The metal and most of its alloys are extremely hard and resistant to scratches. Tungsten has an exceptionally high melting point (3,422 °C), making it impossible to melt without highly specialized smelting equipment. What Are the Applications of Stainless Steel and Tungsten? Are Stainless Steel and Tungsten Both Scratch-Resistant? No, stainless steel offers only moderate scratch resistance and can scratch relatively easily depending on the grade and finish. Yes, stainless steel generally resists cracking well, especially austenitic grades that keep toughness even at low temperatures. No, pure tungsten has poor fracture resistance and is brittle at room temperature due to its high ductile-to-brittle transition. Tungsten alloys with nickel or iron improve toughness and reduce brittleness. Is Stainless Steel Suitable for Shipbuilding? Yes, stainless steel is used in shipbuilding, mainly for fixtures, fittings, and components exposed to seawater, but it is not generally used for major hull structures. Its corrosion resistance and durability make it the obvious choice for various components and structures in ships and boats. While stainless steel is a valuable material in aspects of shipbuilding, the alloy selection depends on exposure to corrosive (salt) conditions. Some grades are entirely unsuited to chloride exposure. Is Tungsten a High-Quality Metal? Yes, tungsten is considered a high-performance metal due to its exceptional density, hardness, and high melting point. Stainless steels are highly corrosion-resistant but can still pit or corrode in chloride-rich or harsh environments. Tungsten resists some chemicals but oxidizes at elevated temperatures and is less corrosion-resistant than stainless steel. How Much Do Stainless Steel and Tungsten Cost? The cost of stainless steel and tungsten can vary widely depending on factors such as the specific grade, form, quantity, and market conditions. Stainless steel prices vary by grade and form, typically from around $2 to $6 per kilogram for common bulk grades, though specialty alloys may cost more. Tungsten is much more expensive, usually around $30 to $60 per kilogram for raw metal, with higher prices for specialized alloys and forms. Is Tungsten as Good as Gold? Tungsten is unrelated to gold in properties or price, though both are very dense metals. Tungsten carbide is sometimes used in jewelry because it is dense, scratch-resistant, and can be polished to an attractive finish. Written by Dean McClements Updated by Audrius Zidonis PhD 16 min read Published January 31, 2024 Updated November 20, 2026 Stainless steel and tungsten are distinct materials with differences in composition, properties, and applications. Stainless steel is an alloy made primarily of iron and chromium, with nickel and other elements added in some grades, and its properties vary depending on the grade. Tungsten is a chemical element with the symbol "W" on the periodic table. It is a transition metal with an exceptionally high melting point and density. Stainless steel is extremely widely used across all industries, including construction, automotive, kitchenware, medical equipment, consumer goods, and outdoor furniture, due to its corrosion resistance and versatility. Tungsten, on the other hand, is used extensively in armor-piercing projectiles, penetrators, and counterweights because of its density and hardness. This article will discuss the key differences between stainless steel and tungsten in terms of composition, types, and applications. What Is Stainless Steel? Stainless steel is a family of alloys, composed of iron, chromium, nickel, and varying amounts of elements like molybdenum, manganese, and silicon. Its remarkable corrosion resistance stems from the formation of a passive chromium oxide layer on its surface when exposed to oxygen. This protective layer prevents rust and deterioration, even in humid or chemically aggressive environments. Stainless steel offers great durability at a relatively low cost, putting this family of alloys at the heart of products in construction, automotive, aerospace, consumer goods, healthcare, industrial processing, and many other sectors. With various grades and types available, stainless steel can be tuned to meet specific requirements, optimizing its value in various applications and more demanding conditions, by careful selection of alloying constituents and heat treatment. To learn more, see our full guide on the Properties of Stainless Steel . What Is Another Name for Stainless Steel? Stainless steel is sometimes referred to as corrosion-resistant steel. It is also called inox, from the French inoxydable, meaning non-oxidizable. What Is Stainless Steel Made Of? Stainless steel’s constituent alloying elements include iron (Fe), chromium (Cr), nickel (Ni), molybdenum (Mo), manganese (Mn), and silicon (Si), with cobalt (Co) only rarely used in specialized grades. The combination and ratios of these alloying agents, along with the manufacturing processes, determine the resulting grade and properties of stainless steel. The divergent grades of stainless steel exhibit alternate crystalline structures that significantly affect the material properties, the level of corrosion resistance, strength, ductility, temperature resistance, and other characteristics. This results in a large family of materials that offer characteristics suitable for a wide range of industrial and commercial applications. How Is Stainless Steel Made? Stainless steels are produced by melting iron with carefully selected alloying elements, primarily chromium, in a controlled furnace process to achieve the desired composition. It begins with a careful selection of raw materials, including iron, scrap steel of known constituents, and selected additions from chromium, nickel, molybdenum, and others. The selection of metals defines the outcome of stainless steel grade and its properties. The selected raw materials are melted in an electric arc or induction furnace at extremely high temperatures. Strict control over temperature and composition is required to achieve precise alloying ratios. Alloying elements are introduced into the molten iron/scrap steel to attain the precise composition needed for the desired grade. These alloying elements are often added in the form of pre-prepared alloy or pure metal ingots. Deoxidizing and desulfurizing agents may be used during the melting process to remove impurities like oxygen and sulfur. Common deoxidizers include silicon, aluminum, and manganese. Sulfur is typically controlled with additives like calcium or rare-earth elements. Samples are taken from the melt for spectroscopic analysis to ensure that the alloying elements are within the specified range. This QC measure guarantees that the final stainless steel product meets industry standards and customer requirements. Once properly alloyed and tested, the molten steel is cast into semi-finished forms such as slabs, billets, or ingots. This can be continuous or batch casting, depending on the scale of production. What Are the Different Types of Stainless Steel? Stainless steel can be classified into several main classes or types based on its microstructure and alloy composition, with fine degrees of differentiation in subcategories of alloys with highly tuned properties. Below are the different types of stainless steel : Austenitic Stainless Steel : These steels are the most common and widely used type of stainless steel. They have a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure and are generally non-magnetic, although they can become slightly magnetic when cold-worked. Renowned for its excellent corrosion resistance, high ductility, and good formability, the common grades include 304 (18-8 stainless), 316 (sometimes called marine-grade), and 321. Ferritic Stainless Steel : They are formed from a body-centered cubic (BCC) crystalline structure. They are magnetic and offer good corrosion resistance, especially in environments with low chloride content. Common grades include 430 and 409. Martensitic Stainless Steel : They transform from austenite to martensite on quenching, giving them a body-centered tetragonal (BCT) crystal structure at room temperature. Duplex Stainless Steel : Duplex stainless steels combine the properties of both austenitic and ferritic stainless steels. They have a mixed microstructure of austenite and ferrite, which provides excellent corrosion resistance and high strength. Common grades include 2205 and 2507 (Super Duplex). Illustration of duplex steel. Precipitation-Hardening Stainless Steel : Precipitation-hardening stainless steels can be heat-treated to achieve elevated levels of strength and hardness. They can be martensitic or austenitic. They are used in applications in which both corrosion resistance and good mechanical properties are critical. Grades include 17-4 PH (martensitic), 15-5 PH (martensitic), 17-7 PH (semi-austenitic), PH 15-7 Mo (semi-austenitic), and JBK-75 (austenitic). Some sources also list FV520, though it is less common. Specialty Stainless Steels : Various specialty grades have been developed for specific applications. Examples include high-temperature grades such as 310 or 446 stainless, low-carbon grades like 304L, and other corrosion-resistant alloys such as Inconel® (though Inconel is not stainless steel but a separate nickel-based superalloy family). Each class of stainless steel has its own optimized properties. Grade selection is crucial to ensuring the resultant product performance and longevity in real-world use environments. What Are the Advantages of Stainless Steel? Stainless steels offer numerous advantages, varied by grade and allowing selection for particular properties that are advantageous for each application: Has exceptional corrosion resistance, making it ideal for harsh environments. Each grade has particular environmental resilience and susceptibilities that can be closely identified. Robust and generally tolerant of wear, impact, and moderately high temperatures, although extreme abrasion or very high temperatures require specialized grades. Provides smooth, non-porous, and durable surfaces that are easy to clean, making stainless steel suitable for food, medical, and pharmaceutical applications. Provide various degrees of mechanical properties, including good tensile strength, though most grades are not as hard as tool steels unless specially treated (e.g., martensitic or precipitation-hardening grades). Adaptable to various industries, from construction and automotive to healthcare and aerospace. Can deliver a sleek appearance and reflective surfaces, making them popular in architectural and decorative applications. Highly recyclable and resistant to process degradation and material loss, promoting sustainability. What Are the Disadvantages of Stainless Steel? While stainless steel offers many advantages across many applications, it also has particular and more generalized disadvantages, such as: It can be more expensive than other materials due to its complex alloy composition and increased difficulty in manufacturing processes. Some grades, such as ferritic and martensitic stainless steels, can become embrittled at low temperatures, while austenitic stainless steels generally retain toughness even in cryogenic conditions. It can be challenging to machine and may require specialized tools and processes. This is particularly true of the austenitic grades, which can demonstrate severe work hardening during cutting processes. Its relatively high density compared to aluminum or titanium makes stainless steel less suitable for weight-sensitive applications. Has lower thermal conductivity compared to other metals like aluminum or copper. Despite this, these materials are often used in heat-exchange applications in which the need for chemical resilience outweighs the thermal limitations. Ferritic and martensitic stainless steels are magnetic, while austenitic grades are generally non-magnetic (though they can become slightly magnetic after cold working), which can affect their suitability for applications such as MRI machines and other sensitive instruments. It can show fingerprints or water spots in a very pronounced way, although they can be easily cleaned. The production of stainless steel can have a significant environmental footprint due to energy-intensive processes and environmentally degrading mining and refining processes. In particular, chromium mining and refining can produce toxic byproducts such as hexavalent chromium, which requires strict environmental controls. Is Stainless Steel Better Than Tungsten? Tungsten is ideal for certain high-wear and very high-temperature applications due to its hardness and high melting point, but it is also denser and significantly more expensive than stainless steel. The ratio of an object's change in length or shape to its original length or shape is known as strain. In many disciplines, including structural engineering, mechanical engineering, and materials science, an understanding of strain is essential because it determines how a material will behave under load, and enables the design of structures that can withstand the expected service stresses. When calculating strain, the amount of material deformation is measured. This deformation is usually expressed as a percentage change in the material's length, area, or volume. Engineers identify several types of strain, based on the kind of stress that produces the particular kind of deformation: longitudinal, lateral, shear, and volumetric strain. Many structures, including bridges, vehicles, and aircraft, experience strain as a result of applied stress in the real world. This article will define strain, its types, and their significance, provide calculation techniques for each type, and give examples of practical applications of strain analysis. What Is Strain in Mechanics? In mechanics, strain is a dimensionless measure of the deformation that a material experiences in response to an external force or load. It is described as the ratio of the change in the material's length or shape to that of the original. Stress, or the force applied per unit area, is related to strain by the material's stiffness or elasticity. Epsilon (ε), the symbol for strain, can be written as a percentage or a fractional value. A fundamental idea in mechanics, strain is important in the planning and evaluation of mechanical systems and structures. What Is the Other Term for Strain? The other word for strain is "deformation", which describes how a material changes in size or shape as a result of the application of a load or force from the outside. In engineering and physics, deformation is commonly used interchangeably with strain and can take many different forms, including stretching, compression, and bending. How Does Strain in Mechanics Work? In mechanics, strain is a concept that describes how a material deforms or changes shape as a result of an external force or stress. Strain is measured using strain gauges, which are tools for detecting and quantifying material deformation. The surface of the material being tested is covered with a grid of fine wire or foil. The strain gauge's wire or foil deforms along with the material being measured, resulting in changes in the gauge's electrical resistance. The degree of strain can be calculated by measuring these variations in resistance. What Is the Importance of Strain in Materials? Strain in materials is important because it explains how materials deform under stress. Designing structures that can withstand expected loads without failing requires a thorough understanding of a material's strain behavior. Strain is used to evaluate a material’s ductility and allows engineers to calculate how much energy a material or structure can absorb when being deformed. What Is the Use of Strain in Mechanics? Engineers use strain as a key parameter to forecast how materials will behave when subjected to loads. Knowledge of the details of strain behavior is essential for the design and analysis of mechanical parts and structures. The main application of strain in mechanics is to comprehend how materials respond to stress. Any time a force is applied to a substance, deformation or a change in shape results. This deformation can be measured in terms of strain. To ensure that structures can withstand the loads they are intended to carry, engineers use strain measurements to assess the strength and stiffness of materials. Mechanical parts like gears, bearings, and shafts are also designed using stress and strain concepts. Engineers can make sure that these parts are sturdy enough to withstand the stresses they will experience during operation by measuring the strain imposed on them by particular levels of stress. How is Strain Measured in Mechanics? Strain gauges and extensometers are the most common methods used to measure both elastic and plastic deformation. Extensometers directly measure a material's change in length, as opposed to strain gauges, which convert mechanical deformation into an electrical signal. Optical methods, such as digital image correlation, can also be used to measure strain by analyzing images of the material under stress. What Are the Units of Strain? The quantity of strain has no dimensions, so it has no units. However, strain is usually expressed as a fractional or percentage change in length. Length changes involved in strain calculations may be measured in meters, millimeters, or micrometers, but strain itself remains unitless. Why Does the Strain in Materials Need To Be Measured? When designing structures that can withstand expected loads, it's important to understand how materials behave mechanically under stress. Structures deform under stress, whether elastically (temporarily) or plastically (permanently). Measurements of strain can also reveal details of material characteristics, such as elasticity, plasticity, and fracture toughness, which are essential for choosing the right materials for engineering applications. What Are the Different Causes of Strain in Materials? There are many causes of strain in materials, including: Mechanical Stress: Mechanical stress is the most common cause of strain in materials. When a force is applied to a material, it undergoes deformation, or strain, which can be either elastic or plastic. Electromagnetic Fields: Certain materials, such as magnetostrictive or piezoelectric materials, can experience strain when exposed to electromagnetic fields due to internal interactions between magnetic or electric fields and their crystal structures. Radiation: When metals are exposed to radiation, they can undergo a process known as radiation hardening. The material may become more brittle but also stronger as a result of this process. As a result, it is less likely to deform under stress, which can result in brittle fractures. The radiation damages the metal's atoms by interacting with them, leading to flaws and dislocations in the lattice structure. This is comparable to other hardening processes like precipitation hardening and work hardening. Fatigue: Fatigue is the gradual weakening of a material due to repeated loading and unloading cycles. This can cause strain in the material, leading to failure over time. Creep: Creep is the slow deformation of a material over time due to a constant load or stress. This can cause strain in the material, leading to failure over time. Manufacturing Processes: Manufacturing processes such as casting, forging, and welding can cause strain on materials due to the high temperatures and stresses involved in these processes. What Are the Different Effects of Strain on Materials? Here are a few typical outcomes of material strain: Elastic Deformation: When a material is subjected to a small amount of strain, it may exhibit elastic deformation. It will return to its original shape when the stress is removed. The amount of strain is proportional to the stress applied, according to Hooke's Law. Plastic Deformation: If the strain applied to a material exceeds a certain threshold, it may undergo plastic deformation. It will remain deformed even when the stress is removed. The material’s capacity to reorganize its atomic configuration without rupturing the interatomic bonds holding it together determines the degree of plastic deformation. Fracture: When a material is subjected to a large amount of strain, it may fracture or break. The amount of dislocation pinning, available slip systems, and atomic bonding in the crystal lattice all affect the amount of strain that can be applied before fracture. Thermal Expansion: Materials may exhibit expansion or contraction in response to changes in temperature. This is known as thermal expansion and can result in significant strains in some materials. Work Hardening: Some materials may become harder and stronger after undergoing plastic deformation. This is known as work hardening or strain hardening and can occur in metals, polymers, and other materials. What Is the Formula for Strain? Strain is a unit of measurement for how much a material deforms in response to stress. Strain is calculated as follows: ε = ΔL / L₀ Where: ε represents strain ΔL represents the change in length of the material L₀ represents the original length of the material Strain is equal to the change in length divided by the original length. This formula is commonly used to calculate strain in materials, such as metals, polymers, and composites. How Is Strain Calculated? The steps in calculating strain (ε) are listed below: Measure the initial length (L0) of the object or material for which you want to calculate the strain. Measure the final length (Lf) of the object or material after it has been deformed. Subtract the initial length from the final length to get the change (the delta) in length: ΔL = Lf - L0. Divide the change in length by the initial length: (ΔL) / L0. Multiply the result by 100 to get the strain as a percentage: ((ΔL) / L0) x 100. Here's an example: Suppose you have a steel wire with an initial length of 10 cm. After stretching it, you measure its length to be 13 cm. L0 = 10 cm (initial length) Lf = 13 cm (final length) Lf - L0 = ΔL = 3 cm (change in length) (ΔL) / L0 = 0.3 (strain as a decimal fraction) 0.3 x 100 = 30% (strain as a percentage) So the strain (ε) in this case is 30%. What Are the Different Types of Strain That Can Occur in Materials? The various types of strains that can develop in materials are as follows: 1. Normal Strain Normal strain describes how a solid material responds to a force that is applied perpendicular to its cross-sectional area. It is measured as the ratio of the change in length to the original length of the material. The formula for normal strain is: ε = ΔL / L₀ Understanding normal strain is crucial for designing and testing materials in various industries. It can help ensure the safety and reliability of structures and products. 2. Tensile Strain Tensile strain is the amount of deformation that a material undergoes when it is pulled or stretched. It is measured as the ratio of the change in length of the material to its original length. The formula for tensile strain is: ε = ΔL / L₀ The measurement of tensile strain is important in materials science and engineering, as it helps to determine a material's ductility and elasticity. 3. Shear Strain Shear strain is a type of strain that occurs when the particles of a material slide past each other in a parallel direction, causing a change in the shape of the material. It is measured as the change in angle between two originally perpendicular lines in the material. The formula for shear strain is given by: γ = tan θ Where: γ is the shear strain θ is the shear angle Shear strain is used in the design of various structures and mechanical systems. 4. Thermal Strain Thermal strain refers to the deformation or change in the size of a material due to temperature changes. Thermal expansion can occur under two different circumstances: non-constrained and constrained. When materials are not constrained, they can move freely in all directions, but when they are, certain directions are restricted, which can cause stress, deformation, or failure. When designing materials and structures, engineers must take into account both conditions to make sure they can withstand the stresses and strains brought on by temperature changes. Thermal strain can be measured using strain gauges or interferometry techniques. The formula for calculating thermal strain is: ε = αΔT Where: α is the coefficient of thermal expansion ΔT is the temperature change Understanding thermal strain is critical in designing and building structures that can withstand temperature variations. Accurate measurement and calculation of thermal strain can help prevent material failure and extend the lifespan of structures. 5. Compressive Strain Compressive strain is the deformation that takes place in a material when it is subjected to a contracting force. Under compression, the space between the atoms of a material is reduced, causing the material to become compacted. It is measured by comparing the original and deformed lengths of a test specimen or structure under compression. The formula for compressive strain is: ε = ΔL / L₀ Compressive strain is important in materials science as it helps determine a material's compressive strength and its ability to resist deformation. 6. Residual Strain The term "residual strain" describes the internal stress that remains in a material after it has been deformed or subjected to external forces. It can be measured using techniques such as X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction. The formula for calculating residual strain involves measuring the change in lattice spacing due to deformation. An accurate measure of residual strain can help an engineer understand the residual stress state in a structure, providing needed information for avoiding potential failures. It can also provide valuable information for improving manufacturing processes and designing structures with enhanced performance. 7. Volumetric Strain Volumetric strain is the term for the volume change that occurs in a material as a result of uniformly applied external forces (hydrostatic strain). It is determined by dividing the volume change by the starting volume. The formula for calculating volumetric strain is: ε = ΔV/V Where: ΔV is the change in volume V is the volume Volumetric strain is important in various fields such as engineering, geology, and materials science. It aids in predicting how materials will react to stress and in designing structures appropriately. “Designing for load is the easy part. Designing for deformation is where it gets complex. Strain dictates whether interfaces misalign, seals fail, or fasteners loosen under cyclic loading. If you're not thinking about strain compatibility between materials and assemblies, you're not thinking long term.” Phillip Keane What Are Examples of Materials Used in 3D Printing, and How Do They Handle Strain? Engineering employs a variety of materials, each of which has particular properties and strain behavior. Here are some examples of material types commonly used in 3D printing, and examples of how they handle strain: Steel: Steel is a common engineering material renowned for its ductility and strength. Steel is the perfect material for high-stress applications like construction, bridges, and heavy machinery because it is ductile enough to accommodate some plastic deformation before final failure. Aluminum: Aluminum is frequently used to take advantage of its light weight and corrosion resistance. Aluminum has a high strength-to-weight ratio and adequate ductility for the kinds of construction, automotive, and aerospace applications that demand consideration of the weight of the structure. Concrete: Concrete is a widely used construction material due to its strength and durability. Although it has a low tensile strength, concrete can handle high compressive loads. Reinforcing materials, such as steel, are added to concrete to increase its tensile strength. Plastics: Plastics are suitable for a variety of applications because they are lightweight and simple to manufacture. They can withstand mild amounts of strain and have good ductility. Plastics are not suited for high-stress applications due to their low strength in comparison to other materials. Ceramics: Ceramics are strong and tough materials that work well in applications where high temperatures and wear resistance are necessary. Ceramics are susceptible to failure under stress because they are brittle and have low ductility. What Are Examples of Polymer Materials Used in 3D Printing, and How Do They Handle Strain? Here are five polymer materials commonly used in 3D printing and their strain-handling characteristics: PLA (Polylactic Acid): 3D printing often uses PLA, a biodegradable and environmentally friendly material. Its moderate tensile strength and relatively high brittleness make it easily breakable when put under stress. ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene): A common material for 3D printing, ABS is a solid and durable plastic. It can withstand moderate strain without breaking because of its relatively high tensile strength. Nylon: A popular material for 3D printing that is both durable and flexible is nylon. It has the highest tensile strength of the polymers mentioned here. When nylon is subjected to strain, it exhibits high elasticity and toughness, meaning that it can stretch without breaking and can absorb significant amounts of energy before failing. PETG (Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol): PETG is a sturdy and durable material that is widely utilized in 3D printing. It has a moderate tensile strength and can withstand moderate levels of strain without breaking. TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane): TPU is a versatile and elastic material that can be utilized in 3D printing. Although it has a low tensile strength, its elastic properties allow it to withstand large amounts of strain without cracking. For more information, see our 3D printer guide . How Does Strain Relate to Stress? Strain is the result of the material's deformation or changes in shape as a result of forces that were applied to it. The elastic modulus of the material describes the relationship between stress and strain. Strain is a measure of deformation, whereas stress is a measure of force per unit area. What Comes First, Stress or Strain? When a material sample is subjected to a force, stress comes first, then strain follows. Stress is defined as the force per unit area applied to an object, whereas strain is the resultant deformation of the object. Stress is the cause, and strain is the effect of stress on the material. What Is the Stress-Strain Curve? A stress-strain curve illustrates how a material responds to an applied force. Figure 1 below is an example of a tensile stress-strain curve: Stress strain curve It is made up of a region where the material is elastic and returns to its original shape, a region where it is plastic and deforms permanently, and a region where it necks and experiences significant deformation and potential fracture. When designing and engineering materials for different applications, it is a crucial tool for engineers and materials scientists. What Is Strain in Hooke's Law? According to Hooke's law, strain is the degree of elastic material deformation that results from the application of a force. In more detail, strain is defined as the ratio of a material’s changed length to its initial length. A material may change in size or shape when subjected to a force, and the amount of strain it undergoes is determined by the strength of the applied force and the characteristics of the material. The modulus of elasticity, also known as Young’s modulus, is a material characteristic that describes how much a material will deform under a specific amount of stress. It describes the relationship between the amount of strain and the amount of stress applied. Mathematically, strain is represented as: ε = ΔL / L₀ What Are the Benefits of Strain Analysis in Mechanics? Among the advantages of strain analysis in mechanics are the following: Ability to predict material behavior under load (evaluation of material properties such as Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio) Design of safe and efficient structures Analysis of deformation and failure mechanisms Optimization of manufacturing processes for specific materials and applications What Are the Limitations of Strain Analysis in Mechanics? The following are some of the limitations of strain analysis in mechanics: External elements like vibration, electromagnetic interference, and other environmental elements can have an impact on strain measurements. This can make it challenging to measure strain accurately in some circumstances. Although strain is an important idea in mechanics, it only represents a small portion of the whole. Other elements, including stress, are crucial in describing how materials behave when they are under load. Strain analysis has limited applicability for nonlinear material behavior, especially when materials do not follow linear-elastic assumptions. Temperature is an additional factor that can (a) cause strain in materials, independent of externally applied forces; or (b) cause the relationship between stress and strain to change with temperature, and become more difficult to predict in some cases. Is Tensile Stress the Same as Tensile Strain? No, tensile stress and strain are not the same. Tensile stress is the amount of force per unit area applied in a direction normal to the cross-section of interest, while tensile strain is the material's elastic or plastic deformation response to the application of a tensile force. However, the two quantities, tensile stress and tensile strain, are related to each other by the elastic modulus of the material. Young’s Modulus, calculated as stress divided by strain in the elastic regime, characterizes a material’s stiffness. Is Shear Stress the Same as Shear Strain? No, shear strain and shear stress are not the same. Shear strain is the shape change caused by an applied shear force, whereas shear stress is the force per unit area applied parallel to a cross-sectional surface of interest. Residual Strain The term "residual strain" describes the internal stress that remains in a material after it has been deformed or subjected to external forces. It can be measured using techniques such as X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction. The formula for calculating residual strain involves measuring the change in lattice spacing due to deformation. An accurate measure of residual strain can help an engineer understand the residual stress state in a structure, providing needed information for avoiding potential failures. It can also provide valuable information for improving manufacturing processes and designing structures with enhanced performance. 7. Volumetric Strain Volumetric strain is the term for the volume change that occurs in a material as a result of uniformly applied external forces (hydrostatic strain). It is determined by dividing the volume change by the starting volume. The formula for calculating volumetric strain is: ε = ΔV/V Where: ΔV is the change in volume V is the volume Volumetric strain is important in various fields such as engineering, geology, and materials science. It aids in predicting how materials will react to stress and in designing structures appropriately. “Designing for load is the easy part. Designing for deformation is where it gets complex. Strain dictates whether interfaces misalign, seals fail, or fasteners loosen under cyclic loading. If you're not thinking about strain compatibility between materials and assemblies, you're not thinking long term.” Phillip Keane What Are Examples of Materials Used in 3D Printing, and How Do They Handle Strain? Engineering employs a variety of materials, each of which has particular properties and strain behavior. Here are some examples of material types commonly used in 3D printing, and examples of how they handle strain: Steel: Steel is a common engineering material renowned for its ductility and strength. Steel is the perfect material for high-stress applications like construction, bridges, and heavy machinery because it is ductile enough to accommodate some plastic deformation before final failure. Aluminum: Aluminum is frequently used to take advantage of its light weight and corrosion resistance. Aluminum has a high strength-to-weight ratio and adequate ductility for the kinds of construction, automotive, and aerospace applications that demand consideration of the weight of the structure. Concrete: Concrete is a widely used construction material due to its strength and durability. Although it has a low tensile strength, concrete can handle high compressive loads. Reinforcing materials, such as steel, are added to concrete to increase its tensile strength. Plastics: Plastics are suitable for a variety of applications because they are lightweight and simple to manufacture. They can withstand mild amounts of strain and have good ductility. Plastics are not suited for high-stress applications due to their low strength in comparison to other materials. Ceramics: Ceramics are strong and tough materials that work well in applications where high temperatures and wear resistance are necessary. Ceramics are susceptible to failure under stress because they are brittle and have low ductility. What Are Examples of Polymer Materials Used in 3D Printing, and How Do They Handle Strain? Here are five polymer materials commonly used in 3D printing and their strain-handling characteristics: PLA (Polylactic Acid): 3D printing often uses PLA, a biodegradable and environmentally friendly material. Its moderate tensile strength and relatively high brittleness make it easily breakable when put under stress. ABS (Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene): A common material for 3D printing, ABS is a solid and durable plastic. It can withstand moderate strain without breaking because of its relatively high tensile strength. Nylon: A popular material for 3D printing that is both durable and flexible is nylon. It has the highest tensile strength of the polymers mentioned here. When nylon is subjected to strain, it exhibits high elasticity and toughness, meaning that it can stretch without breaking and can absorb significant amounts of energy before failing. PETG (Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol): PETG is a sturdy and durable material that is widely utilized in 3D printing. It has a moderate tensile strength and can withstand moderate levels of strain without breaking. TPU (Thermoplastic Polyurethane): TPU is a versatile and elastic material that can be utilized in 3D printing. Although it has a low tensile strength, its elastic properties allow it to withstand large amounts of strain without cracking. For more information, see our 3D printer guide . How Does Strain Relate to Stress? Strain is the result of the material's deformation or changes in shape as a result of forces that were applied to it. The elastic modulus of the material describes the relationship between stress and strain. Strain is a measure of deformation, whereas stress is a measure of force per unit area. What Comes First, Stress or Strain? When a material sample is subjected to a force, stress comes first, then strain follows. Stress is defined as the force per unit area applied to an object, whereas strain is the resultant deformation of the object. Stress is the cause, and strain is the effect of stress on the material. What Is the Stress-Strain Curve? A stress-strain curve illustrates how a material responds to an applied force. Figure 1 below is an example of a tensile stress-strain curve: Stress strain curve It is made up of a region where the material is elastic and returns to its original shape, a region where it is plastic and deforms permanently, and a region where it necks and experiences significant deformation and potential fracture. When designing and engineering materials for different applications, it is a crucial tool for engineers and materials scientists. What Is Strain in Hooke's Law? According to Hooke's law, strain is the degree of elastic material deformation that results from the application of a force. In more detail, strain is defined as the ratio of a material’s changed length to its initial length. A material may change in size or shape when subjected to a force, and the amount of strain it undergoes is determined by the strength of the applied force and the characteristics of the material. The modulus of elasticity, also known as Young’s modulus, is a material characteristic that describes how much a material will deform under a specific amount of stress. It describes the relationship between the amount of strain and the amount of stress applied. Mathematically, strain is represented as: ε = ΔL / L₀ What Are the Benefits of Strain Analysis in Mechanics? Among the advantages of strain analysis in mechanics are the following: Ability to predict material behavior under load (evaluation of material properties such as Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio) Design of safe and efficient structures Analysis of deformation and failure mechanisms Optimization of manufacturing processes for specific materials and applications What Are the Limitations of Strain Analysis in Mechanics? The following are some of the limitations of strain analysis in mechanics: External elements like vibration, electromagnetic interference, and other environmental elements can have an impact on strain measurements. This can make it challenging to measure strain accurately in some circumstances. Although strain is an important idea in mechanics, it only represents a small portion of the whole. Other elements, including stress, are crucial in describing how materials behave when they are under load. Strain analysis has limited applicability for nonlinear material behavior, especially when materials do not follow linear-elastic assumptions. Temperature is an additional factor that can (a) cause strain in materials, independent of externally applied forces; or (b) cause the relationship between stress and strain to change with temperature, and become more difficult to predict in some cases. Is Tensile Stress the Same as Tensile Strain? No, tensile stress and strain are not the same. Tensile stress is the amount of force per unit area applied in a direction normal to the cross-section of interest, while tensile strain is the material's elastic or plastic deformation response to the application of a tensile force. However, the two quantities, tensile stress and tensile strain, are related to each other by the elastic modulus of the material. Young’s Modulus, calculated as stress divided by strain in the elastic regime, characterizes a material’s stiffness. Is Shear Stress the Same as Shear Strain? No, shear strain and shear stress are not the same. Shear strain is the shape change caused by an applied shear force, whereas shear stress is the force per unit area applied parallel to a cross-sectional surface of interest.
